# VR Looter-Shooter Dungeon Crawler – Unreal Engine Project Plan

## Project Overview

This project is a **VR looter-shooter dungeon crawler** built in Unreal Engine for Meta Quest 3. It combines elements from roguelikes and action RPGs to deliver endless dungeons, intense combat, and addictive loot collection. Key features include:

- **Procedurally Generated Dungeons:** Infinite labyrinths assembled from modular 3D room tiles for fresh layouts every run【9†L85-L93】. A random seed drives each dungeon, so levels can be regenerated deterministically for synchronization or daily challenges【9†L119-L127】.
- **Deterministic Loot System:** Diablo-style item drops with rarity tiers (common, magic, rare, legendary, etc.), random stat affixes, and fixed item seeds for reproducibility【20†L1-L4】. No two drops are identical, yet any item can be consistently re-generated from its seed and definition.
- **Modular Gear & Crafting:** Weapons and gear are constructed from multiple components (blades, hilts, barrels, etc.), allowing items to be disassembled into parts and reassembled into new gear. Players can craft, upgrade, or swap parts to customize equipment.
- **Loot Boxes & Vending Machines:** Gacha-style **loot box** mechanics and in-game vending machines provide booster packs and random pulls. Players spend in-game or premium currency for a chance at rare loot, with **deterministic outcomes** based on a seed to ensure fairness【24†L139-L142】.
- **AI “Game Master” Director:** An AI director monitors player performance and dynamically adjusts the game. It delivers on-the-fly quests/events and tunes the difficulty by spawning enemies or pickups, ensuring a balanced, unpredictable challenge【27†L683-L691】【27†L694-L702】.
- **Voxel Destructible Environments:** Minecraft-like destructible terrain built from voxel blocks. Walls, floors, and objects can crack and collapse under explosions or tools, using a chunked voxel system optimized for Quest mobile VR【9†L133-L142】.
- **Comfortable VR Locomotion:** Multiple movement options including smooth locomotion (“sliding”), teleportation, snap-turn rotation, and dash maneuvers. These ensure VR comfort by minimizing motion sickness (with vignetting, blink teleport, etc.) while preserving fast-paced action【19†L67-L70】.
- **In-App Purchases & Currencies:** The game supports a premium currency for microtransactions (e.g. buying loot boxes or cosmetics). In development builds this is stubbed out for testing, but it’s designed for easy integration with Oculus/Meta in-app purchase APIs.

Beyond the client features, the project includes a robust **backend on AWS** for persistence and multiplayer. Player data, items, and world states are stored in DynamoDB, while AWS Lambda services and GameLift servers handle the online economy and co-op dungeon sessions. All systems are described in detail below, with an emphasis on how to implement them in an Unreal Engine project.

## Unreal Engine Setup & Project Structure

We will use **Unreal Engine 5** (with OpenXR) to target the standalone Meta Quest 3 headset. Unreal’s VR template and XR plugins will be enabled to provide baseline VR controller support and tracking. Key setup steps:

- **Project Configuration:** Create a new UE5 project (Blueprint or C++ as needed) and enable the **Oculus OpenXR** plugin for Quest compatibility. Configure Android platform settings for Quest 3 (ARM64, Vulkan/OpenGL ES, etc.) and use mobile-forward rendering or Vulkan for optimal performance on mobile hardware. We’ll disable expensive engine features (e.g. ray tracing) and use baked lighting or simple lighting models to maintain 90Hz VR performance【5†L19-L27】.
- **Folder Structure:** The Unreal project (e.g. *EchoDungeonVR.uproject*) will be organized with folders for Maps, Blueprints, and Assets. For instance:  
  **Content/**  
    **Maps/** – procedural dungeon levels (entry room, etc.)  
    **Blueprints/** – gameplay systems (DungeonGenerator, ItemSystem, VRPlayer, AIDirector, etc.)  
    **Blueprints/Items/** – item data structures, loot generation logic  
    **Blueprints/VR/** – player pawn, VR locomotion components, UI widgets (3D menus)  
    **Meshes/** and **Materials/** – modular room pieces, weapons, props, voxel block meshes  
    **Data/** – JSON or DataTable assets for item definitions (from the HALO “Digital Pill” data) and loot tables.  
  This structure makes it easy to manage the various systems and content in an exportable Unreal project folder.
- **VR Framework:** Utilize Unreal’s VRTemplate or XR Interaction components for baseline VR interaction. The VR pawn will have components for head (camera) and motion-controller hands. We will integrate locomotion logic (teleportation, smooth movement) into this pawn. UI will be handled via World Space Widgets or 3D widgets attached to the player (for menus like inventory or vending machine interfaces, appearing as in-world panels【2†L55-L58】).
- **Meta Quest 3 Build:** Set up the Android packaging settings to deploy to Quest 3. This includes configuring the Oculus Mobile SDK or OpenXR for VR, setting the correct texture compression (ASTC), and enabling *arm64* packaging. We will test iteratively on the Quest via USB (using `adb install` to sideload builds). In release, the project can be packaged as an APK and delivered either through the Oculus Store or sideloaded from a secure URL (we plan to host builds on S3 for testing convenience【24†L301-L309】).

With the project foundations in place, we next detail each major feature and how to implement it in Unreal.

## Procedural Dungeon Generation (Modular Tiles)

To provide endless dungeon layouts, we implement **procedural 3D dungeon generation** using modular room pieces【9†L85-L93】. The level is built by snapping together pre-designed room and corridor segments in an algorithmic fashion:

1. **Modular Room Library:** Create a library of room prefabs – e.g. chambers, hallways, intersections – each built as a reusable level fragment. Each prefab has defined **doorway exit points** tagged with connector types (e.g. a corridor end vs. a room entrance)【9†L91-L99】. For example, a corridor segment might have “corridor” type connectors that can attach to a “room” type doorway.
2. **Generation Algorithm:** Start dungeon generation with a starting room (spawn room) that has multiple exits. Then iteratively fill exits: for each open doorway, randomly select a compatible module from the library and attach it. The new piece is rotated and positioned so its entrance aligns with the open connector【9†L101-L109】. Once placed, mark that doorway as filled and add any new exits from the piece to the list of open connectors【9†L109-L117】. Continue until the dungeon reaches the desired size or until no open connectors remain.
3. **No Overlap & Boundaries:** During placement, we perform collision checks to prevent overlap between modules. We can also impose boundaries (e.g. a maximum radius or room count) to keep the dungeon within performance limits【9†L115-L123】. If an attachment would go out of bounds or intersect existing geometry, we skip and try a different piece or terminate that branch.
4. **Deterministic Layout Seeds:** The generator uses a random **seed** value to drive all random choices (module selection, maybe orientation). Using the same seed will produce the same layout every time【9†L119-L127】, which is crucial for multiplayer synchronization and allowing daily challenge dungeons. The seed can be derived from a global “world seed” or provided by the server for consistency.
5. **Populating Content:** After layout generation, we spawn gameplay elements in the dungeon. Each room module can have predefined marker points for enemies, chests, traps, etc. We then randomize spawns at those markers (e.g. place monsters appropriate to the dungeon depth, scatter some destructible crates, etc.). These spawn events can also be seeded for determinism, or orchestrated by the AI Director (see below). The result is a unique, interconnected 3D labyrinth assembled like a puzzle from hand-crafted pieces【9†L125-L133】, giving designers control over individual rooms while keeping overall layouts unpredictable.

This modular approach ensures **replayability** – *“players will never run out of dungeons to explore”* due to the countless combinations of room pieces【9†L127-L132】. Yet each dungeon feels designed, not completely random, because the content of rooms is authored. Unreal Engine implementation will likely use an Editor Script or a runtime procedure in the Level Blueprint or Game Mode to construct the dungeon at level start. We’ll also prepare a fallback fixed level for testing, but ultimately the goal is that every session generates a new dungeon.

## Deterministic Loot & Item Generation (Diablo-Style)

Loot in the game draws heavy inspiration from **Diablo-style** item systems, featuring multiple rarity tiers and randomized stats【11†L199-L207】【11†L219-L222】. The core principle is that every item drop is generated **deterministically** from a known seed and rule set, ensuring both fairness and reproducibility. Key aspects of the loot system include:

- **Item Base Types & Rarities:** We define a catalog of base item types (e.g. *sword*, *axe*, *pistol*, *chest armor*, etc.), each with intrinsic properties (base damage range, attack speed, defense, etc.)【11†L221-L228】. Items come in rarity tiers (common, magic, rare, legendary, mythic, etc.), which govern the number of **affixes** (random bonus properties) and overall power range【17†L273-L280】. For example, a *Rare Sword* might get 2–3 random affix rolls, whereas a *Legendary Sword* has 4 affixes plus a unique legendary effect.
- **Procedural Affixes:** When an item of Magic rarity or higher is generated, the system rolls a set of affixes for it. Affixes are chosen from a pool appropriate to the item type and level: e.g. a sword might roll bonus % damage, strength, life steal, elemental damage, etc.【17†L265-L273】. The number of affixes depends on rarity (Magic gets 1, Rare 2-3, etc.). Each affix has a random value within a range (e.g. “Ferocious” might give +20–50% damage)【17†L267-L275】. We ensure affixes are valid for the item (no “increase bow draw speed” on a sword, for instance, by tagging affixes with allowed item types【17†L269-L272】). The item’s level (tied to dungeon depth or enemy level) influences the affix strength – higher level drops yield higher stat ranges, and some affixes won’t appear below certain item levels【17†L273-L281】.
- **Deterministic Item Seeds:** Every generated item is associated with an **item seed** (an integer or GUID) that encapsulates its randomness. All the random decisions (base type selection, affix choices and values) are derived from this seed and the current loot generation rules. This means each “drop” or crafting outcome can be reproduced exactly given the same seed and version of loot rules【20†L1-L4】. For example, if a chest generates an item with seed `123456`, the game (or server) can re-run the item generation algorithm with that seed to verify the result. This determinism is crucial for server-authoritative drops and preventing client-side tampering.
- **Item Data Structure:** Under the hood, items are represented as structured data objects (we can use Unreal Data Assets or a JSON schema) containing their core fields: base type, rarity, level, affixes, components (for crafted items), etc. For instance, a generated item might be stored as: `{id: "sword001", type: "Sword", level: 10, rarity: "Rare", affixes: [ {...}, {...} ], seed: 98765}`【17†L297-L305】. We will leverage the **HALO Digital Pill** schemas provided to define this structure. According to the HALO item schema, each item includes fields for base type, rarity, level, a list of component IDs, and an affix list, all tied to a seed【1†L203-L211】. Using such a structured definition makes it easy to serialize items, network them to other players, or store them in the database, since we can just transmit the key fields or the seed to recreate the item on another machine【17†L297-L305】.
- **Example – Item Generation:** Suppose the loot system decides to drop a weapon and rolls a *Magic Sword* at level 1. The base type “Sword” defines the base damage, say 5–10. Magic rarity allows 1 affix. The generator picks an affix by random: e.g. “*of Flames*” which adds fire damage on hit【17†L299-L307】. It rolls the magnitude for that affix (say +5 fire damage). The final item might be *“Sword of Flames” (Level 1, Magic)* with base damage ~7 (roll within 5–10) and +5 fire damage. Internally it might have `seed=12345` and an item hash for identity. Another playthrough with the same seed and parameters would produce the same *Sword of Flames*. As players progress to deeper levels, higher rarities and more affixes come into play – *“No two legendary items are 100% the same”* due to the random affix rolls on top of unique effects【17†L279-L287】.

To summarize, **loot generation is both excitingly random and rigorously deterministic**. The randomization provides variety and surprise (e.g. chasing that perfect roll on a legendary), while the determinism (seed-based generation and server verification) ensures a fair economy and allows features like ghost replays or daily seed challenges. We will implement the item generator as an Unreal Blueprint or C++ module that takes a seed and produces an Item Data Asset, referencing the predefined base stats and affix tables (which designers can tweak externally in a data file or spreadsheet【17†L307-L314】 for balancing). All item drops, whether from chests, enemies, or gacha pulls, will use this unified generator.

## Modular Gear Components & Crafting System

An innovative aspect of the game is **modular gear** – many items consist of interchangeable parts. For example, a rifle might have a stock, barrel, and scope component; a sword might have a blade and hilt. Players can dismantle loot to reuse parts and craft new items, adding a creative **crafting loop** on top of random drops.

**Item Components:** Using the HALO schema definitions, each item’s makeup is a set of components (each with an ID and type)【1†L203-L211】. Component types (as defined in the schema) include things like *blade*, *hilt*, *trigger*, *barrel*, *bow_string*, *arrow_head*, *enchantment*, etc.【1†L19-L27】. Each component carries its own stats or traits – e.g. a “blade_iron” component might contribute +8 damage and have a trait “balanced”【1†L139-L147】, while a “hilt_oak” might add +2 stability (handling)【1†L157-L163】. An assembled sword item that uses those components will have the combined stats of blade + hilt, plus any magical affixes on the item. This modular approach means items are essentially **recipes** of parts.

**Crafting & Assembly:** To craft a new item, the player chooses a **blueprint** or base item type (e.g. the blueprint for “Longsword” expects 1 blade component and 1 hilt component). In the crafting interface, the player would select compatible components from their inventory to fill each required slot. We enforce slot compatibility by tags or types (you can only put a “blade” kind component into the blade slot of the sword blueprint, etc.)【22†L1-L4】. Once all slots are filled, the new item can be assembled: the system deterministically generates a new item ID/seed from the combination of components and perhaps a crafting RNG. The resulting item gets a new item_hash identity and inherits stats from all components. For instance, assembling *blade_iron + hilt_oak* yields a basic Iron Sword. If desired, a crafting RNG seed could also introduce minor variability (or affixes) so that two swords made of the exact same parts aren’t identical, but that would be deterministic via the seed as well.

**Disassembly:** The reverse is also possible – any modular item can be disassembled, breaking it back down into its component parts. This allows players to salvage a valuable component from a junk item or to mix-and-match parts between items. Disassembly yields the original component items (which go into the player’s component inventory) and possibly some **salvage materials** (a small reward like scrap metal or arcane dust) as a byproduct【22†L1-L4】. Salvage materials could be a secondary resource used for other crafting actions (like upgrading item rarity).

**Reassembly & Part Swapping:** An advanced feature is the ability to **swap components** on an existing item – essentially a partial re-craft. For example, if you have a great sword with a mediocre blade, you could remove the blade and attach a better one (say, a “dragonsteel blade”) onto the hilt. The item would then update its stats to reflect the new blade and receive a new item_hash (since its core composition changed). This operates similar to assembling a new item, but possibly preserving certain item metadata. After reassembly, the item’s seed or hash is recomputed due to the changed part, ensuring uniqueness【22†L1-L4】. The game would treat it as a new item instance (and log the change in the provenance ledger).

**Enhancements & Enchanting:** In addition to mixing physical parts, the crafting system may allow enchantment or modification of items. For example, a crafting station might allow players to spend resources to **reroll one affix** on a rare item, or consume some rare materials to **upgrade an item’s rarity** (turn a Rare into a Legendary with some risk). As noted in design references, Diablo 3’s enchanting system is a good model – letting players mitigate RNG by re-enchanting one property【17†L288-L296】. We will incorporate a limited form of this: e.g. using a special crafting token to randomly change one affix on an item, or combining duplicate items to improve one of them. These actions are also deterministic given the inputs (e.g. fixed seed for reroll), but give players a sense of agency in item improvement beyond pure luck【17†L288-L296】.

The **crafting UI** will be implemented as an interactive VR workbench. Players can pick up item parts and slot them into a holographic outline of the target item. Once all parts fit, a “Forge Item” button (or a dramatic lever pull in VR) triggers the assembly. Disassembly could be as simple as placing an item into a disassembly station which then outputs its components. Under the hood, the Item System will handle validating combinations and updating item data. All crafted or modified items still go through the deterministic generation pipeline – for instance, crafting might internally generate a new item seed or use a hash of component IDs to ensure consistent results. We will also update the **provenance log** for items: every time an item is crafted, disassembled, or modified, an entry is added (e.g. “Item X crafted from components A, B” or “Item Y disassembled into A, B”)【21†L1-L4】. This ties into the backend for item tracking (see Backend section).

## Loot Boxes & Vending Machines (Gacha Mechanics)

The game integrates **gacha/loot box mechanics** in a VR-friendly way to enhance the loot collection excitement. There will be in-world **vending machines** and loot crates that players can interact with to receive random items or packs. These systems are implemented with careful attention to both fun and fairness:

- **Vending Machines:** Scattered in safe zones or at dungeon entrances, vending machines allow players to spend regular in-game currency (earned from enemies or quests) to buy supplies and item packs. For example, a machine might sell a **“Weapon Part Pack”** for 100 credits which yields a random weapon component, or a **health potion** for 50 credits (fixed item). Each vending machine can offer a menu of items: some **fixed purchases** (known item for a price) and some **randomized purchases**【24†L136-L142】. The randomized ones are essentially loot box pulls – e.g. “Lucky Dip box: costs 200 credits, rewards a random Rare or better item.” The machine is represented as a 3D object; the player would press a button or insert virtual coins, and the item would dispense (perhaps physically dropping out for the player to catch or pick up, adding a tactile VR element).
- **Loot Boxes / Gacha Pulls:** In addition to vending machines, certain loot chests in the dungeon or a special **gacha shrine** allow the player to spend **premium currency** (or earned tokens) for a high-reward random item. This is analogous to opening a loot box or doing a gacha pull in other games. The outcomes and probabilities are configured in loot tables (with drop rates for rarities). Crucially, each pull is **deterministic under the hood** – the randomness is driven by a seed that can be provided or verified by the server【24†L139-L142】. This prevents exploitation and aligns with the deterministic item generation: if the server says “this loot box opened with seed X”, both client and server will generate the same reward item from that seed. In practice, for single-player offline play the client can generate it, but for online integrity we’ll have the server validate or even send the result.
- **Booster Packs:** The game might offer multi-item loot packs (like opening a booster pack of cards). For instance, a “Module Booster Pack” could give 3 random weapon components, or a “Legendary Pack” might guarantee one legendary item out of 5 draws. These will be implemented as a sequence of gacha draws in one go, with a nice VR animation (e.g. the player opens a container and several items fly out). Each pack will have a predefined composition (quantity and rarity guarantee) and use its own seed(s) to roll items.
- **Visual & UX Design:** Opening loot in VR should be a **spectacle**. When a loot box is opened, we’ll spawn the item(s) with some physics impulse so they **tumble out onto the floor** realistically【11†L199-L207】. For example, a chest might pop open and coins and gear burst out, bouncing slightly (using Unreal physics) before coming to rest for the player to pick up【11†L199-L207】. We’ll use particle effects and sound to enhance this moment (a brief celebratory burst that doesn’t overwhelm performance)【11†L195-L203】. After a short time or once the items are collected, any remaining physics objects will settle and disable physics to avoid ongoing cost【11†L205-L213】.
- **Economy and Fairness:** We will be transparent with drop rates (to comply with loot box regulations). The premium **token currency** required for gacha can be earned slowly in-game or purchased via IAP (see next section). We also include measures to ensure players aren’t severely disappointed by bad luck – e.g. a pity system where after many pulls without a legendary, the chance increases. All random draws are logged (and, if online, could be auditable on the backend) to maintain an honest economy.

In summary, the vending/gacha system adds an extra layer of excitement and player agency – you can **gamble your earnings for a chance at something great**. But thanks to deterministic seeds and server oversight, it will *“always produce an item seed”* that can be tracked and verified【20†L1-L4】. From an implementation standpoint, vending machines will likely be Blueprint actors in the level that contain an array of item definitions or loot tables. When activated, they either dispense a predefined item (for fixed buys) or call the Loot Generator with a random seed for a roll. Gacha shrines might interface with the backend (for deducting premium currency and recording the drop) then trigger the same local item spawn logic. We will also create attractive 3D UI panels on these machines for players to select purchases in VR (e.g. a floating screen with item icons and prices).

## AI Director: Dynamic Quests & Difficulty Adjustment

To keep the gameplay experience dynamic and responsive, we incorporate an **AI Director** system (a virtual Dungeon Master). This system acts behind the scenes to adjust the game’s pacing, difficulty, and even generate impromptu quests based on the player’s situation【27†L683-L691】. The AI Director ensures that the dungeon never feels too predictable or too easy/hard for long stretches:

- **Dynamic Difficulty Balancing:** The Director continuously monitors the players’ status and performance – health levels, combat efficiency, time since last challenge, etc.【27†L706-L714】 – and makes adjustments on the fly. Its goal is to maintain a fun **“dramatic arc”** in the gameplay【27†L689-L697】. For example, if the players are cruising through without taking damage, the Director might **trigger an ambush** in the next room or spawn an extra wave of monsters to ramp up the challenge. Conversely, if the players are struggling (low health, recent close calls), the Director can **dial down the difficulty** by delaying enemy spawns or even spawning a helpful health pickup or ammo cache【27†L694-L702】【27†L728-L732】. This kind of dynamic difficulty adjustment keeps tension balanced – avoiding long monotony but also preventing unfair overwhelms.
- **Adaptive Spawning & Events:** The Director influences what events happen throughout the dungeon. In practical terms, before the player enters a room, the AI Director decides what that room should contain. The same room layout might sometimes be empty (a breather), other times hold a swarm of enemies or a mini-boss, or maybe a trap and a treasure. The decisions are weighted by the current dramatic tension and randomness【27†L701-L709】. For example, *“sometimes an ambush occurs in a particular room, other times that room stays quiet but later a boss spawns unexpectedly”* – this ensures even if the map layout is known, the encounter content is unpredictable【27†L701-L708】. The Director can also spawn side objectives or quests: e.g. spawn an NPC prisoner to rescue if things have been too combat-heavy, or trigger a timed challenge if players have been idle.
- **Quest Generation:** Beyond combat pacing, the AI Director may generate dynamic micro-quests to guide the player. These could be context-based (“You hear a roar in the distance – find and slay the elite monster”, if the player is doing well) or assistance-based (“Find a healing fountain – you are gravely wounded”, if the player is in trouble). Quests are delivered via brief voice-over or text prompts in the HUD. The completion of these ad-hoc quests yields rewards (health, loot drops, etc.) that help reinforce the desired pacing (e.g. giving a struggling player a path to recover).
- **Implementation:** The AI Director can be implemented as a singleton object (perhaps a subsystem or part of the GameMode). ## VR Locomotion & Comfort Options

Comfortable and immersive locomotion is **paramount in VR**, so our game offers multiple movement schemes to accommodate different player comfort levels【19†L7-L15】【19†L19-L27】. We implement a combination of smooth movement and teleportation, along with various comfort enhancements, so that players can choose what works best for them:

- **Smooth Locomotion (“Slide”):** The player can move continuously using the analog stick on the VR controller, as in a traditional FPS (forward/back/strafe). For realism and comfort, movement speed is capped to a reasonable walking/running pace (e.g. ~1.5 m/s walking, ~3 m/s running)【19†L13-L21】 to prevent excessive vection discomfort. We include comfort options such as a **vignette** (tunnelling effect) that darkens the periphery of the view during movement【19†L19-L27】 and an optional **“stepwise” movement** mode where smooth motion is broken into a rapid series of micro-teleports (which some users find reduces motion sickness). Smooth locomotion provides high immersion, especially for combat, but all these toggles are there to make it as comfortable as possible.
- **Teleportation:** For players very sensitive to motion, we offer standard VR teleportation. By pressing a button, the player can arc a laser pointer and choose a destination within a certain range; releasing instantly blinks the player to that spot. This completely eliminates translational movement discomfort. We will use a blink transition (fast fade-out/in) so the teleport is smooth. Teleport can be balanced in gameplay by limiting its range or frequency (e.g. a short cooldown), but since this is a PvE game, we can allow fairly liberal teleport to ensure anyone can play comfortably.
- **Snap Turns:** Smoothly turning the view can be disorienting in VR, so we implement **snap turning** for reorientation. When the player pushes the turn stick (or presses a rotate button), the view will rotate a fixed angle (e.g. 30° or 45°) instantaneously or with a very quick fade, instead of a continuous yaw. Snap turns prevent the inner-ear/vision mismatch that causes dizziness. We will allow the angle to be configurable or allow smooth turn as an option for those who tolerate it.
- **Dash/Dodge Move:** As part of gameplay, we include a short **dash** ability. This is a quick burst movement (a few meters in the direction the player is moving or looking). It can be used to dodge enemy attacks or close gaps. The dash is designed to be **VR-friendly**: it’s very quick and could be coupled with a slight screen blur or blink during the motion to reduce discomfort【19†L37-L39】. Because it’s instantaneous (<0.5s) it tends not to cause motion sickness and adds a fun locomotion mechanic for combat. We bind dash to a button (or double-tap on the stick) and give it a short cooldown.
- **Customization:** All locomotion options are configurable. In a VR **Settings Menu**, players can choose their movement mode (Teleport, Smooth, or even enable both), turn on/off vignetting, adjust snap turn angle, and toggle features like “Comfort Dash”. The idea is to let the user tailor the experience. By default, we might start new users in a comfort mode (teleport + snap) and let them graduate to smooth if they wish. Throughout development we’ll test these modes with users to ensure the game can be comfortably enjoyed by a wide range of players【19†L43-L51】【19†L67-L70】.

Unreal Engine’s input system and VR templates give a good starting point for these locomotion mechanics. We will likely use an enhanced version of the built-in VR pawn: adding a **NavMesh**-driven teleport system (with a parabola arc visualization), implementing snap turns via a simple yaw rotation on the camera rig when input is received, and using character movement component for smooth locomotion. The dash can be implemented by a quick impulse or teleport with a screen fade. By providing and refining these options, we ensure the fast-paced dungeon crawl action remains accessible and **comfortable** in VR, fulfilling Meta’s guidelines for VR locomotion preferences【19†L67-L70】.

## Voxel-Based Destructible Environments

The dungeon environments aren’t just static—they’re **destructible**. We employ a **voxel-style terrain** system to allow players (and explosions) to break walls, floors, and other structures in the dungeon, adding a layer of emergent gameplay (creating new paths, uncovering secrets, or just causing mayhem). However, we must balance destruction with performance, especially on Quest hardware, so our approach is a hybrid one:

- **Voxel Chunk System:** We represent destructible sections of the environment as composed of medium-sized **blocks** rather than fully detailed tiny voxels. For example, dungeon walls might be made of 0.5m or 1m cubic chunks that can be individually destroyed【9†L139-L147】. These chunks can be instanced static meshes or a procedural mesh component in Unreal. We partition the world into **chunks** (regions) so we can load/unload or update smaller sections as needed, rather than tracking thousands of individual cubes at once【24†L153-L161】. Non-destructible architecture (like certain floors or key pillars) will remain as normal static meshes to keep complexity down.
- **Material Properties & Damage:** We will define a variety of material types for voxels – e.g. stone, wood, metal, glass, dirt – each with properties like hardness, resistance to certain damage types, etc.【24†L148-L156】. For instance, stone blocks might have high resistance to physical damage but low resistance to explosive damage; wood might burn or break easier. Each voxel block will have an HP value derived from its material’s strength. When players hit a block (with a weapon or explosive), we apply damage to that block. If using Unreal’s Chaos physics, we might not simulate each block physically until it breaks; we simply keep track of health.
- **Progressive Destruction Stages:** Rather than blocks simply disappearing when hit, we implement **destruction stages** for better visuals and feedback. A block can be: **Intact** (no damage), then after some damage switch to a **Cracked** state (we can swap its material or overlay a cracked texture), further damage -> **Fractured** state (visibly very broken, maybe with holes or an alternate mesh), and finally **Broken** (block is removed)【24†L155-L163】. For performance, we might not simulate partial meshes but instead have a small number of pre-broken variants or use decals. The final removal of the block either deletes it or replaces it with some debris pieces.
- **Physics Debris:** When a block breaks, we can spawn **debris** (chunks of rock or wood) that fall to the ground for visual effect【9†L143-L151】【24†L163-L166】. However, we will limit the physics cost: use object pooling for debris, limit the number of active rigid bodies, and possibly switch to simplified physics on the Quest (e.g. debris that vanish after a few seconds)【24†L163-L166】. Larger structures might use *Chaos fracture* – for example, a large destructible pillar could be a single mesh that breaks via a precomputed fracture pattern. But for general walls and terrain, the voxel chunk approach is simpler to network and reset.
- **Networking & Persistence:** In multiplayer, when a block is destroyed, we need to sync that with all players. We’ll have the server authorize and broadcast block destruction events. We maintain a record of destroyed blocks (e.g. storing their coordinates in a `WorldDeltas` log in DynamoDB for persistence between sessions)【24†L209-L214】. New players joining mid-session or respawning will be informed of which blocks are missing. Because we use a deterministic layout seed, we know the initial state of all blocks; the server only needs to transmit changes (deltas). Unreal’s replication system or a custom RPC can handle this: possibly using a bit grid or list of removed blocks in the GameState for efficiency (since Quest can handle some replication but we must be mindful of bandwidth).
- **Optimizations:** We won’t attempt to make the entire dungeon fully destructible at a tiny scale – that would be too many objects. Instead, we strategically designate areas for destructibility (e.g. certain walls that hide secrets, or all rocks in a cave section). This ensures we have enough gameplay use (like mining or breaking through a shortcut) without overwhelming the engine. We may also implement **structural integrity** checks: for example, if a player digs out all blocks under a ceiling chunk, the ceiling might collapse as one piece. But full physics-based structural support is expensive, so we might keep it simple or on a local level (small cave-ins)【24†L159-L164】. The system will be tuned so that destruction is fun and impactful (e.g. blasting a hole in a wall is satisfying) while staying within Quest 3’s limits by using relatively **large voxels and chunked updates**【9†L139-L147】.

Overall, the destructible environment adds to the **immersive sandbox feel** – players can alter the map, create new paths or hazards (imagine blowing up a bridge as enemies cross it), and the world feels interactive. By leveraging a voxel-like approach with chunking, progressive damage visuals, and debris pooling, we ensure it’s performant. We will test destruction-heavy scenarios on Quest to keep frame rates steady, adjusting chunk sizes or limiting simultaneous destruction if needed. This feature also integrates with the loot and AI systems: e.g. enemies might drop mining charges for the player to open blocked areas, and the AI Director might trigger a cave-in behind the player to push them forward, etc., making the dungeon feel alive.

## Backend Services & Multiplayer (AWS Cloud Integration)

To support persistence, multiplayer, and the in-game economy, we deploy a suite of backend services on **Amazon Web Services (AWS)**. This backend handles everything from player data and item databases to matchmaking for co-op sessions. Below is an outline of the cloud components and how they interact with the game:

- **DynamoDB Data Storage:** We use Amazon DynamoDB (a NoSQL database) to store all persistent game data, structured into multiple tables for different entities. The key tables include:  
  - **Players** – Stores player profiles with fields like player_id (primary key), currency balances (credits, premium tokens), and timestamps【24†L189-L195】.  
  - **Items** – Stores every persistent item by a unique item_hash (primary key). Each entry includes the owner_id (which player has it), the full item JSON or data (for backup/verification), an optional server signature, and timestamps【24†L189-L195】. This ensures that even rare items are tracked.  
  - **Provenance** – An append-only log of item events, keyed by item_hash (partition key) and timestamp (sort key). Every time an item is created, modified, traded, etc., a record is added here describing the event【24†L195-L202】. This gives a “history” for each item (useful for preventing dupes and implementing the blockchain-like audit trail).  
  - **Listings** – Represents marketplace listings for items. Primary key is a listing_id, storing fields like seller_id, the item_hash being sold, type of listing (auction or fixed-price), price, end time, and current state (active, sold, canceled)【24†L197-L202】.  
  - **Bids** – For auction-type listings, this table stores bids. Partition key is listing_id, sort key is timestamp (or bidder_id), with each entry logging a bid amount and bidder_id【24†L197-L202】. This helps resolve auctions and identify winners.  
  - **BuyOrders** – Stores “want to buy” orders placed by players (if we allow players to request items). Each entry might have an order_id, buyer_id, criteria (e.g. “any sword of at least Rare rarity”), quantity, price offered, and state【24†L203-L211】. The market service can match these against listings.  
  - **WorldDeltas** – Stores changes to the world/dungeon state (for persistent or long-running worlds). Partition key is a world_id or dungeon run ID, sort key timestamp. Each entry logs an operation like a block destruction or a door unlocked, including position and details【24†L209-L214】. This can be used to reconstruct or replay changes, or persist world modifications between sessions.  

  These tables together support the game’s needs for persistence. For example, when a player picks up loot, the item can be recorded in Items (with item_hash as key) and a provenance entry “dropped by monster X at time Y” is added【21†L1-L4】. When a player lists an item for sale, an entry goes to Listings, etc. DynamoDB is chosen for its scalability and ability to handle high-throughput with low latency, which is ideal for a global game economy.

- **AWS Lambda Microservices:** We implement the backend logic using **serverless functions (Lambda)**, which are lightweight and cost-effective. Each major domain has its own Lambda function (or set of functions), encapsulating the logic for that part of the game【24†L215-L223】:
  - **Player Service:** Handles player account creation, profile lookup, and currency updates. E.g. `POST /player/create` to initialize a new profile, `POST /player/spend` to deduct or add currency (with server checks to prevent cheating)【24†L231-L239】. It ensures players’ credits/tokens can’t go negative and might award daily login bonuses, etc.
  - **Item Service:** Responsible for item generation and validation. For instance, when the client “opens” a loot drop, it can request `POST /drop/request` which triggers the server to generate a random seed and return it (and a commit hash)【24†L233-L240】. The client then uses that seed to generate the item locally. The client must then call `POST /item/register` with the resulting item data; the service verifies the item’s stats match the expected seed outcome and then stores it in the Items DB and returns a **signature**【24†L233-L240】. This signature (HMAC of item data) is saved with the item, so any future verification can prove it was server-authorized【24†L223-L231】. This Lambda essentially acts as the “authority” for all loot outcomes and item integrity.
  - **Market Service:** Implements the in-game marketplace logic. Endpoints include listing an item for sale (`POST /market/list`), canceling a listing, buying out a listing (`POST /market/buyout`), placing a bid on an auction (`POST /market/bid`), creating or canceling a buy order, and browsing listings【24†L236-L243】. The service will update DynamoDB tables accordingly and enforce rules (e.g. you can’t buy an item from yourself, bids must be higher than last, etc.). When a sale completes, it will transfer ownership of the item in the Items table and credit the seller’s account.
  - **World Service:** Handles persistent world changes. It might have endpoints like `POST /world/delta` to record a change (like a voxel destroyed or a puzzle solved) and `GET /world/delta/{world_id}` for clients joining to fetch what’s changed【24†L238-L245】. For a session-based dungeon, this might not be heavily used (changes may not persist after the run), but for any shared or long-lived worlds it’s useful. It can also be used to store user-generated content or level edits if that becomes a feature.

  Each Lambda is stateless, relying on the DB for state. They will be written in Python 3.11 (as indicated) for quick development【24†L185-L193】, using a common library for tasks like authentication and item validation. We will bundle these in an AWS SAM or CloudFormation template so they can be deployed easily (the Codex plan even included a `template.yaml` and `deploy.sh` script for automating this【2†L73-L81】【2†L85-L93】).

- **API Gateway:** All the above services are exposed to the game client via an **API Gateway** (HTTP REST API). We define routes corresponding to the service functions, e.g.:  
  `POST /player/create`, `GET /player/{player_id}`, `POST /player/spend` for player service;  
  `POST /drop/request`, `POST /item/register` for item drops【24†L231-L239】;  
  Marketplace routes like `POST /market/list`, `/market/buyout`, `/market/bid`, `/market/browse` to fetch listings【24†L236-L243】;  
  and world routes like `/world/delta`【24†L238-L245】.  
  The API Gateway will use Lambda Proxy integration to route calls to the appropriate Lambda. We will secure these endpoints initially with a simple API key or token in headers for dev/testing【24†L247-L249】. Before launch, we plan to integrate a proper authentication system (possibly AWS Cognito with JWTs or verifying Oculus user tokens) so that each request is tied to a valid player session. The API Gateway provides a single URL (domain) that the game client can be configured with, making HTTPs calls to interact with the backend.

- **Multiplayer Servers (GameLift/EC2):** While small-scale co-op could potentially be peer-to-peer, we aim to support more robust **dedicated servers** for dungeon instances. AWS GameLift is a service tailored for deploying game server binaries and managing matchmaking/lobbying. GameLift can keep a fleet of these servers ready and spin up new ones on demand. GameLift allocates a server process and returns the connection info (IP/port) to the clients. The players’ game instances then connect to that server and play together in the dungeon. The server authoritative model ensures that physics (like voxel destruction, enemy AI, item drops) are synchronized and cheat-resistant. We will integrate basic GameLift APIs in the client to handle session creation and joining. As a fallback or for development, we can also allow hosting a server on a standard EC2 instance or even listen-server hosting by one of the clients (Unreal’s replication can handle this, though for Quest that’s less common). The dedicated server will utilize the same dungeon generation with the given seed, so all players see the same layout. We will leverage Unreal’s replication framework for gameplay: for example, the server holds the true state of items and uses replication to show item drops to players, and uses RPCs to handle player actions (shooting, hitting a voxel, etc.). We will also ensure server performance is optimized (e.g. running at a tick rate that Quest can keep up with). GameLift provides scaling – if many parties are playing, it will run multiple servers; if not, it will scale down to save cost.

- **Build Distribution (S3):** During development and testing, we plan to use Amazon S3 to host game builds (APK files) and perhaps updates. We can upload each test build to an S3 bucket and share a link with testers, or use it in conjunction with a simple patcher. Additionally, S3 might be used to store any large dynamic content (like user-generated dungeon presets, if any, or logs). 

All these cloud components ensure that the game has a **persistent world and economy**. Players’ progress is not lost between sessions – their inventory, currency, and achievements are stored server-side. The **marketplace** is enabled by having a central database and services to list/search items globally. The **integrity** of the loot system is guarded by server logic (signing drops, verifying crafts) so that even in a looter economy, cheating is minimized and item trading can thrive with trust. We will also set up monitoring (CloudWatch logs, metrics) and have admin tools to balance the economy (e.g. adjust drop rates via a config that the item service uses, without needing a client patch). - **Performance Tuning:** We enforce a budget of **72–90 FPS** on Quest 3. This involves careful profiling using tools like the Oculus OVR metrics or Unreal’s stat sheets. If needed, we will scale down certain effects on Quest: e.g. limit the number of active physics objects (sleeping excess loot as described)【11†L207-L214】, use simpler shaders or static lighting, reduce the voxel chunk update rate, etc. Quest 3 is more powerful than its predecessors, but we still treat it like mobile hardware in terms of optimization.
- **Quality Settings:** We will provide a couple of quality presets (perhaps default vs. battery-saver) where we can adjust things like foveated rendering level, density of particle effects, and maybe disable ambient occlusion or other effects to maintain frame rate. - **Testing Procedure:** Every major feature implemented (locomotion, combat, crafting, destruction) will be tested on-device with real users if possible. ## Overview and Inspiration
The project is a **2D pixel-art dungeon crawler** for Android/iOS, inspired by the earlier 3D *EchoForgeVR* looter-shooter concept. Like its VR predecessor, this game will feature **fast-paced loot collection and modular gear crafting** – but reimagined in a retro pixel-art presentation. Players will delve into procedurally generated dungeons, defeat enemies, and collect deterministic loot (with Diablo-style rarity tiers and random affixes). Core design pillars include: 
- **Procedural dungeon generation** (randomized layouts built from room “modules”),  
- **Deterministic loot drops** with **item seeds** and rarity/affix system,  
- An in-game **gacha/loot-box vending machine** for bonus item pulls,  
- **Modular item crafting** (assemble gear from component parts, with disassembly),  
- **Cloud-backed persistence** using AWS (Lambda, DynamoDB, API Gateway) for saving player data and item provenance.

The game is **single-player (solo mode)** only – networking is used solely for cloud saves and ensuring item integrity, not for multiplayer gameplay.

## Engine Choice and Project Setup

Godot’s scene system and tilemap support make procedural generation easier to implement, and it can export directly to APK (Android) and Xcode project (iOS) with minimal overhead. Unity is also an option (with its robust mobile support and larger community), but it may introduce more bloat and longer iteration times for a pixel-art game of this scale. 

**Why Godot:** Godot is open-source, has an instant-play editor for quick testing, and excels at 2D rendering and physics. It allows scripting in GDScript (high-level Python-like language) which is quick to write and modify. The engine’s small build size will keep the APK lightweight. Additionally, Godot’s **Mobile export** templates make generating an Android APK or an iOS Xcode project straightforward. For example, we can script an automated export for both platforms in CI. If Unity were chosen instead, we would use Unity 2023 with the 2D URP pipeline – but given our pixel-art style and need for agility, Godot is preferable.

**Project Structure:** The project will be organized for clarity and modifiability. In Godot, we’ll create a `dungeon` folder for generation logic, an `items` folder for item scripts and data, and so on. If following the *EchoForgeVR* blueprint, we will include both a game client and a backend folder:
- A `godot/` directory containing the Godot project (scenes, scripts, assets).
- A `server/` directory with AWS Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) templates (e.g. SAM or CloudFormation) and Lambda function code (for persistence, etc.).

## Procedural Dungeon Generation (Rooms & Layout)
The game will feature **randomly generated dungeons** composed of pre-designed room modules stitched together in unpredictable layouts each run. The approach is to use **room “chunks”** (small hand-crafted maps or templates) that can connect at doorways, ensuring fast content creation and variety. This “chunk-based” procedural generation is a common and effective technique: it yields immediate playable results by placing pre-made rooms on a grid and connecting them, as seen with tools like Unity’s DunGen【27†L139-L147】. We’ll leverage this approach to get visually coherent yet random levels:

- **Room Module Library:** We will design a library of room prefabs (e.g. corridors, treasure rooms, monster lairs, boss chambers). Each module will have defined entrance/exit door positions on its edges. For example, a corridor piece might have doors at both ends, whereas a dead-end room has one door. By keeping modules on a grid (e.g. 10×10 tiles each), they can snap together cleanly.
- **Layout Algorithm:** The dungeon generator will start with a starting room and iteratively attach new rooms to free doorways. A simple algorithm: place a starting room at the center, then keep a list of open door positions. Randomly pick an open door and attach a random room module that fits (matching doorway types). Continue until a desired number of rooms is placed. We’ll ensure no overlapping by keeping track of occupied grid cells for each room. This method is efficient and has been proven in many roguelikes – it’s similar to algorithms described on RogueBasin and by Buck/Angband for sprinkling rooms then connecting them【24†L139-L147】.
- **Corridors & Connectivity:** If two rooms don’t directly connect, the generator will place corridor pieces (hallways) to bridge gaps. Alternatively, some room modules can include corridor sections. We aim to **always create a fully connected dungeon** (every room reachable) – no isolated sections. A connectivity check (e.g. flood-fill from the start) will verify this, and extra corridors can be added if needed.
- **Random Features:** Within the generated layout, we’ll add random features: locked doors, traps, secret rooms, etc., to increase variety. These can be sprinkled after the basic layout is complete. The dungeon size, room count, and enemy distribution can scale with player progress (deeper levels = more rooms and tougher foes).

The result will be a fresh dungeon each playthrough, but made of familiar pieces. This **modular procedural design** offers the best of both worlds: handcrafted feel with random arrangement. It also makes development easier – we can create a new room design in the editor and add it to the pool without touching code. Each dungeon run will be identified by a seed value so that generation is **deterministic** if needed (for debugging or daily challenge modes, the same seed can reproduce the same layout). 

## Loot Generation and Item System
Loot in this game is heavily inspired by **Diablo-style randomized items**. Every weapon, armor, or gadget drop will have a **base type** (e.g. “Longsword”, “Laser Rifle”, “Leather Armor”) and then a set of randomly rolled attributes (affixes) determined by its rarity. We will implement a **deterministic loot generation** system where each dropped item is reproducible from a known *seed*. This means the random rolls are not truly random each time – they’re tied to a seed value saved with the item. This has several benefits: consistency between client and server, prevention of item “re-roll” exploits, and the ability to uniquely identify items.

**Rarity & Affixes:** Items will come in rarity tiers (common, uncommon, rare, epic, legendary, etc.), each influencing how many affixes (prefixes/suffixes) the item gets and the stat ranges. For example, a *common* sword might just have base damage, while a *rare* sword could have +Fire Damage and +Attack Speed affixes. We’ll define affix pools similar to Diablo’s: e.g. prefixes like “Flaming” (adds fire damage) or “Heavy” (more damage but slower), suffixes like “of the Titan” (+Strength) etc.【38†L115-L123】. The affixes and their values are rolled via a pseudo-random number generator (PRNG). With a deterministic approach, when an item drops, the game will generate a random **item seed** (likely a 32-bit or 64-bit number). Using this seed as input, the loot generator will pick affixes and values. The **item’s seed is then stored** in its data. If needed, the server or any client can re-run the same generation function with that seed to get the same outcome【38†L31-L38】.

**Deterministic Generation:** As noted, randomness in computers is actually deterministic given a seed. We will leverage that: *“Random is a complicated function which is deterministic. Seed can be complicated… you can mash timestamp, player ID, etc.”* to produce unpredictable but replayable results【35†L270-L279】. In practice, our loot drops might use a combination of factors to create a unique seed: e.g. the dungeon run’s overall seed, plus the monster ID and time of drop. This ensures two players won’t get the same loot unless by design, but if we needed to **replay** a specific drop (for debugging or to validate a trade on the backend), we could. 

Every item in the database will include its `item_seed` and a version stamp for the generation rules. The loot generation code (either on client or server) can thus regenerate an item’s properties from these inputs【38†L33-L40】. This determinism is particularly useful for verifying item legitimacy in an online setting – although our game is solo, we plan to future-proof the system for potential online features. For example, the backend can impose server-side rolls for critical drops to prevent cheating. In a similar fashion, a developer on Blizzard’s forum explained that in *Diablo 3* a loot table/seed might be generated at character creation to predetermine drops【35†L162-L170】 – we won’t go that far, but we’ll ensure each drop is *decided at drop time and then fixed*.

**Item Identity & Provenance:** To support persistence and prevent item duplication cheats, each item will have a unique **hash identifier**. Using the deterministic data, we compute an `item_hash = SHA-256(canonical_json(item_core_fields))` – effectively a fingerprint of the item’s stats and seed【38†L37-L45】. This hash (or a shorter GUID derived from it) serves as the item’s ID. We also maintain a **provenance log** per item 【38†L37-L40】: an append-only history of actions (e.g. item dropped by monster X at time Y, player crafted it, disassembled it, etc.). This is similar to a blockchain ledger but without the overhead of actual blockchain – it’s just a server-verified log for each item. For now, this log will live in DynamoDB for persistence. Every time an item changes (crafted, traded in gacha, etc.), a new event is appended. This way, if we ever introduce trading or a player economy, we have a built-in record of item origin and transformations.

**Example:** A *“Rare Plasma Rifle”* drops from a boss. The game rolls an item seed `0xAB3D...` which yields base damage 40, plus affixes *“Burning”* (+5 fire damage) and *“Sniper’s”* (+10% crit chance). The item is saved with seed `AB3D...` and hash ID `HMAC_SHA256(seed+stats)`. If the player later disassembles this rifle, the provenance log might record “Disassembled into components A, B, C at 10:32 UTC”. All this info is stored in the backend. It’s important to note that while item generation can be done client-side for responsiveness, we will **validate or even perform critical rolls on the server** for integrity when saving. In fact, one practice from online games is to do random generation on the server to prevent tampering【34†L185-L193】. We can implement a hybrid: the client generates loot for instant feedback, but on save, the server re-generates from the seed and ensures the item stats match before accepting the save (and could overwrite if discrepancy is found). This maintains a seamless experience while keeping the server authoritative over item stats.

## Gacha System: Vending Machine Loot Boxes
To add excitement and a monetization angle, the game will include a **gacha/loot-box mechanic** in the form of a *vending machine or shrine* in the dungeon hub. Players can spend special tokens (earned in gameplay or via IAP in a F2P scenario) to get a random item roll. This system is analogous to loot boxes in other games – a random reward with a chance at high-rarity loot. The term **“gacha”** comes from Japanese capsule toy machines (Gashapon) which dispense random toys of varying rarity【36†L81-L90】. Our implementation will be designed to be fun and not predatory, staying within platform guidelines (e.g. we will disclose drop rates if required by App Store policies).

**How it Works:** In the starting town or between dungeon levels, the player finds a vending machine or mystical shrine. Interacting with it presents options to spend tokens for a **loot pull**. For example: *“Spend 1 Token for a random Rare or better item”* or *“Spend 5 Tokens for 5 pulls + guaranteed Epic”*. When the player confirms, the game will trigger the loot generator to create a new item (or bundle of items) using the same deterministic system as enemy drops. The difference is that the **loot table is controlled**: the gacha might have certain item types or quality bias. For instance, the shrine could be “Weapon Voucher” that guarantees a weapon drop of at least Rare quality. We will implement this by defining special loot generation rules for the vending machine. It may simply call the normal item generator with an enforced minimum rarity parameter (e.g. ensure the random roll *meets or exceeds a rarity threshold*)【38†L109-L117】.

Importantly, **gacha pulls will also be deterministic and seed-based**. Every pull produces an item with a seed and we log it just like any drop. If done online, the server can generate the item upon request (preventing any possibility of client “rerolling” by resetting the game). The design is such that even *premium* loot is part of the same deterministic ecosystem – ensuring fairness and traceability. In fact, we can treat the gacha machine as simply another loot source, but one that a player pays tokens to use. The probabilities for each rarity tier from the machine will be clearly defined (and likely displayed to the user to comply with loot box transparency regulations).

From an implementation standpoint, the **vending machine node** in-game will have a script to handle purchases: when player interacts, it checks token currency, calls an item generation function (possibly contacting a Lambda function to record the transaction and get a server-trusted random seed), then dispenses the item to the player’s inventory. Visually, we can add some flair – e.g. an animation of the machine and an item popping out with a glow corresponding to its rarity. But since speed of iteration is key, we will start with a simple UI popup for the result and add polish later.

This system adds a long-term progression element (collect tokens for pulls) and a sink for any premium currency if we introduce it. Even though our initial focus is not heavy monetization (the project can be premium or free with optional IAP), it’s wise to design this now. Gacha systems are prevalent in top-grossing mobile games for good reason – when done ethically, they provide thrill and reward for players, and revenue for developers【36†L93-L102】【36†L109-L117】. We’ll balance it by ensuring that all loot from gacha is obtainable through normal play as well (gacha just gives a chance sooner).

## Modular Item Crafting System
One standout feature of EchoForge (both VR and this 2D version) is the **modular item crafting**. Gear isn’t just static loot – it can be broken down into components and rebuilt in new combinations. This adds depth to the loot hunt: players can mix-and-match parts to forge the perfect weapon, or salvage junk items for parts to use elsewhere.

**Item Composition:** Each equipment item will be made up of **components**. For example:
- A sword might consist of a *Blade* component and a *Hilt* component (and perhaps a *Gem* slot).
- A firearm could have components like *Barrel*, *Receiver*, *Stock*, *Magazine*, etc.
- Armor could have *Armor Plating* plus an *Insignia* or *Lining* component.

When an item drops, it comes with randomly generated components that together define its stats. For instance, a “Longsword of Flames” item might have a Blade part that gives base damage and fire damage, and a Hilt part that adds accuracy and strength. In our data model, an Item will contain a list or tree of its component objects【38†L115-L123】. Each component can itself have quality levels and possibly affixes. This is similar to how *Warframe*’s modular weapons (Kitguns, Zaws) are crafted from parts that determine the final stats【32†L13-L17】, or how *Borderlands 3* guns are composed of manufacturer parts. 

**Crafting & Assembly:** At a crafting station (e.g. in the hub town), the player can perform:
- **Disassembly** – break an item down into its component parts. This destroys the item and yields its components back into the player’s component inventory. Some loss or “salvage” might occur (we could have a chance a component is destroyed or converted to raw materials), but initially we can do a 1-to-1 return for simplicity.
- **Assembly** – take a set of components and combine them into a new item. The player would choose a “blueprint” or item template (e.g. choose to craft a Sword, or a Gun of a certain class), then select appropriate components for each required slot. The system will validate that the chosen parts are compatible with the blueprint (e.g. you can’t put a *bowstring* on a sword) – each component and slot will have tags or IDs to enforce this. Once the parts are in place, the player crafts the item, and the components are consumed, producing a new item in inventory【38†L125-L133】.
- **Reassembly (Modding)** – instead of full crafting, the player can also **swap a component** on an existing item. For example, take a Sword and swap its Blade for a different Blade component. This effectively *re-rolls* some of its stats while keeping other aspects. Under the hood, this is similar to disassemble the item (removing one component) and then assemble a new one with a new component while keeping others. We will implement it as a convenient UI: e.g. “Replace Barrel with [Better Barrel]”. The item’s seed and hash would change because the item’s core fields changed (and we log this in provenance as an item modification event)【38†L129-L133】.

When crafting or modding produces a new item, we will generate a **new deterministic seed for the new item** and compute a new hash ID【38†L129-L133】. This ensures that even crafted items fit into the deterministic loot framework – you could even imagine “craft seeds” that yield the same result if repeated, though here it’s more about combining parts.

To support this system, we’ll maintain a **Component Inventory** for the player (separate from full items). The UI will likely need tabs for “Items” and “Components”. Many components will be generic (e.g. an “Iron Sword Hilt” could drop from any disassembled sword), encouraging players to dismantle extra loot. Rare components might only come from disassembling high-end items or as special drops. There’s a satisfying loop here: loot -> break down -> craft -> new loot. We will be sure to clearly present the stats contributed by each part in the crafting interface, so players can theorycraft combinations.

From a coding perspective, modular items mean we need a flexible item data structure. In Godot, for example, we might have an `Item` class that contains an array of `Component` objects. Each component has its properties and possibly methods. When computing final item stats, we sum up or combine effects from all components. We might tag some components as “Cosmetic” vs “Functional” so that e.g. a sword’s visual sprite can be composed of blade + hilt images layered together if we get that detailed – but to start, we may just use a single composite sprite per item and not dynamically draw it (to keep art simpler, the combination effect will be mainly in stats).

**Design Balance:** We will need to balance this system so that it’s neither too trivial (e.g. always obvious what the best part is) nor overwhelmingly complex. A likely approach is to have **component tiers**. Basic Iron components yield normal stats, while rare Mythril components yield higher stats plus maybe special effects. Crafting might require a small gold fee or material to prevent free infinite swapping. But these details can be fine-tuned with playtesting. The core goal is to empower players to tinker with their gear, extending the lifespan of each drop (a “junk” drop might have one great part worth keeping).

## Backend Persistence and Cloud Architecture
Although the game is solo, we are implementing a robust **backend on AWS** to persist player data, ensure determinism, and prepare for possible future online features (like trading or leaderboards). The backend stack will use **AWS Lambda (serverless functions)**, **Amazon DynamoDB (NoSQL database)**, and **Amazon API Gateway** to expose RESTful endpoints to the game. This architecture aligns with the plan from the VR version (which included an AWS deployment)【38†L13-L15】, but we’ll simplify to what’s needed for single-player persistence initially.

**Data to Persist:** Player profile and progression (e.g. character stats, completed dungeon levels), inventory of items and components, and the provenance logs of items will all be stored in DynamoDB tables. DynamoDB is a great fit because it’s schema-flexible (we can store item JSON directly) and scales serverlessly with demand. We can have tables such as:
- `Players` table (keyed by PlayerID) – stores basic profile and maybe a list of item IDs they hold.
- `Items` table (keyed by ItemHash or ItemID) – stores the item data blob (seed, stats, components, provenance log). This could be large, but DynamoDB can handle items up to 400KB which is plenty.
- Optionally `Components` table if we want to store components separately (but we can also embed component info in the Items blob to start, since components are only acquired via items or crafting).

Each play session, the game will retrieve the player’s data from the cloud and save back any changes. For example, when you finish a dungeon and return to town, a Lambda could be invoked to update your inventory and progress.

**Serverless API:** We will create **Lambda functions** for key operations: e.g. `SaveInventory`, `LoadInventory`, `CreateNewItem`, `LogProvenanceEvent`, etc. These will be written in Python or Node.js (Python is convenient for quick development). They interact with DynamoDB using AWS SDK. API Gateway will provide HTTPS endpoints that the game client calls. Because this is a mobile game, we will also integrate **AWS Cognito** for authentication – each user will log in (possibly implicitly if we allow an anonymous identity or Game Center/Google Play sign-in) and obtain credentials to call the APIs securely【34†L131-L139】. This prevents anyone from abusing the endpoints without auth.

**Example workflow:** When an item is looted in-game, the client immediately shows it (to avoid lag). Then, in the background or on next save point, the client calls `POST /items` with the item data (or seed) to a Lambda. The Lambda verifies/generates the official version of that item (ensuring the deterministic generation matches the seed and perhaps applying a server signature if we require) and stores it in the `Items` table【38†L41-L45】. It also updates the player’s inventory record to include the new item’s ID. If we implement gacha or crafting, those actions also go through Lambdas so the server can subtract currencies, remove consumed components, and create new items – all in a transaction to maintain consistency.

We will script the **deployment** of this backend using IaC. Likely we’ll use AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model) with a template YAML (as hinted in the VR script)【38†L73-L82】. This template defines our DynamoDB tables and Lambda functions. A `deploy.sh` script (as in the VR plan) will package and deploy the stack to AWS with one command. This means any collaborator can spin up their own backend instance easily. We’ll include instructions on obtaining AWS credentials and deploying in the documentation.

**Offline Mode:** If the player is offline, we will cache their progress locally (perhaps in a small JSON save file) and then sync with the backend next time they’re online. ## Project Overview 
This project is a **2D dungeon crawler** game inspired by *EchoForge*, built with Unity’s 2D URP and targeting **Android and iOS** platforms. It features **procedural generation** for dungeons, loot, and item visuals, a deep item crafting/disassembly system, a gacha-style lootbox mechanic, and offline-capable solo gameplay. On the backend, it integrates with AWS serverless services (Lambda, DynamoDB, API Gateway) to support player data, item management, an item marketplace, and persistent world changes. All cloud infrastructure is defined via **Infrastructure-as-Code** (AWS SAM templates) and includes scripts for one-step deployment. The deliverables include the full Unity project folder (with C# scripts, placeholder art assets, and JSON data files), sample mobile build outputs, and comprehensive README documentation for both setting up the Unity project and deploying the AWS backend.
