# Modular 2D Dungeon Crawler Engine Architecture

**Overview and Goals:** We propose a **clean-slate 2D dungeon crawler engine** built with highly modular systems, enabling easy composition and mod support. The engine’s design emphasizes **emergent complexity** – complex gameplay arising from simple interacting rules【21†L55-L63】. Every core feature (dungeon generation, loot, combat, magic, crafting, etc.) is an isolated module with a clear interface, so developers or modders can extend or swap parts without breaking others. By separating concerns in this way (similarly to an ECS architecture), the engine remains *flexible, scalable, and data-driven*【15†L211-L219】. All content (levels, items, quests, enemies) is procedurally generated from rules rather than hard-coded, ensuring infinite variety. The engine supports both **pixel and voxel-style** graphics with features like biome blending, seamless tile transitions, post-processing effects, and a tile-based **fog-of-war** system for exploration. Aesthetic themes (cyberpunk, dark fantasy, sci-fi, etc.) are not hardwired – art assets and parameters for each can be plugged in, allowing the **rendering module** to apply different tilesets or shaders per theme. We target a *single buildable codebase* that can deploy to desktop or Android (using a framework such as **Phaser 3** for web/Android, **MonoGame** for C#, **Love2D** for Lua, or **Python+PyGame** for rapid prototyping). Below, we outline the project architecture, module interfaces, and initial subsystem implementations ready for testing and expansion.

## Architecture Overview (ECS and Module Design)

To maximize modularity and emergent behavior, we adopt an **Entity-Component-System (ECS)**-like architecture for the engine core. In an ECS, *entities* (game objects like players, monsters, items, tiles) are just unique IDs or containers, *components* are data buckets (health, position, sprite, etc.), and *systems* are the logic that operates on entities with certain components【15†L211-L219】. This separation of data and behavior allows us to treat each major feature as a *system module* that can be developed and tested in isolation, then plugged into the engine. It also enables dynamic composition: we can add or remove components from entities on the fly to change their behavior without rewriting class hierarchies【15†L211-L219】. This is ideal for an open-ended simulation game – for example, to apply a burning effect to an object, we just attach a “OnFire” component and let a FireSystem handle the burning logic, rather than hard-coding fire behavior into every object class.

**Module Isolation and Interfaces:** Each core subsystem is implemented as a **self-contained module** (likely a class or set of classes) with a well-defined interface or API. Other parts of the engine communicate through these APIs or through an event bus, rather than directly poking into each other’s internals. This means, for instance, the **DungeonGeneration** module can produce a `DungeonMap` data structure (e.g. a 2D array of tile types and metadata) which the **Rendering** module takes to draw the level, and which the **AI** or **Physics** modules use for pathfinding and collision. The **LootSystem** module might expose a function `generateLoot(context)` which other systems (combat or chests or gacha) call to get a random item appropriate to a context (enemy level, chest rarity, etc.). By coding to interfaces, we could replace the entire loot generation logic with a modded version (say, switching from fantasy loot to sci-fi loot) without affecting the rest of the engine – as long as it adheres to the same interface contract.

**Event-Driven Interaction:** To support rich interactions across systems (and potential user mods), the engine can include a simple event messaging system. Systems can emit events (e.g. “entity moved”, “attack landed”, “item picked up”) that other systems listen for. For example, the Physics module might emit a “entity collided” event that the Combat system listens to in order to apply fall damage, or the Magic system could broadcast “spell cast” which the Sound or Particle system picks up to play effects. This decoupling ensures systems remain **independent** yet cooperative in creating gameplay outcomes.

**Data-Driven and Mod-Friendly:** All game content and rules are defined in external data files or scripts (JSON, Lua scripts, etc.) rather than hard-coded. For instance, item components, enemy stats, spell definitions, loot drop tables, terrain biomes – all can live in data assets that are loaded at runtime. This means new items, monsters, or even entirely new magic schools can be added by editing data or adding a script, without recompiling the engine. In practice, we might organize the project with directories like `data/` (for JSON/CSV defining items, affixes, monsters, etc.), `assets/` (for image/sound files, possibly grouped by theme), and `scripts/` (for mod scripts or the Haloic magic language spells). The engine reads these on startup to configure each module. This design aligns with the philosophy of some modern engines where modularity is key – e.g. Thunder Engine emphasizes being able to include/exclude modules as needed and letting developers create custom modules to extend the engine【11†L351-L359】.

**Core Modules Overview:** The key subsystems/modules in this engine include:

- **Dungeon Generation Module** – Procedurally creates dungeon layouts (rooms, corridors, terrain features) with tunable parameters for endless variety.
- **Terrain & Physics Module** – Manages the physical properties of tiles and entities (collision, gravity if any, projectile physics) and handles environment interactions (e.g. liquids, fire propagation).
- **Fog-of-War & Vision Module** – Tracks what tiles have been seen by the player (or other vision sources), for dynamic fog-of-war rendering.
- **Loot & Item System Module** – Generates items and loot drops using a component+affix system; manages item database and crafting/disassembly logic.
- **Affix & Elemental Logic** – Handles item affixes and elemental effects (like fire damage, poison, etc.), including how elements interact (e.g. water puts out fire).
- **Combat System Module** – Orchestrates turn-based combat mechanics, including turn order, attack resolution, damage calculation, and status effects.
- **Magic System Module (Haloic Language)** – Interprets or executes spells written in the custom *Haloic scripting language*, producing magical effects within the game world.
- **Enemy AI Module** – Governs enemy behavior (patrol, chase, attack) possibly via behavior trees or state machines, and uses pathfinding on the dungeon grid.
- **Rendering Module** – Responsible for drawing the world: tilemap rendering, sprite animations, UI, post-processing effects (shaders for lighting, color grading, etc.), and applying the fog-of-war overlay.
- **Gacha System Module** – (Optional) Provides a “loot box” style mechanic where players can spend currency to receive random item rewards, leveraging the loot generator with specific probability tables.

Each of these modules can be thought of as an ECS *system* or a service. They operate on shared data structures (the world entities and components) or on data passed through interfaces. Now, we’ll go into each major subsystem in detail, describing the design and showing initial code prototypes where applicable.

## Dungeon Generation Module

**Purpose:** The dungeon generator module creates the game’s levels on the fly, using procedural algorithms rather than fixed maps. It must be highly configurable (“knobs and levers”) to produce a wide range of layouts – from cramped caves to sprawling castles – depending on the desired theme or difficulty【13†L119-L127】. This supports the requirement for varied aesthetics and ensures no two runs are the same.

**Approach:** We treat the dungeon as a grid of tiles (e.g., a 2D array of cell types). The generator can use a mix of algorithms: for example, **rooms-and-corridors** generation for indoor dungeons, cellular automata for caves, or even prefab “chunks” stitched together for special areas. To maximize reuse, the module can implement a *base algorithm* (or several selectable algorithms) with parameters for room size, corridor length, sparseness, loopiness, etc. Indeed, a known approach in roguelikes is to have multiple algorithms and tune them per area instead of writing bespoke generators each time【13†L119-L127】. For instance, one area might use more open rooms and loops, another area uses labyrinthine corridors – all by tweaking parameters or switching sub-algorithms while using the same generator code.

**Data Structures:** The output of this module is a `DungeonMap` object containing:
- A 2D array or matrix for the terrain grid (each cell might be an enum or code: wall, floor, door, water, etc.).
- Metadata like list of room regions (each with coordinates, for placing things or for AI navigation), spawn points for player/exit, etc.
- Possibly connectivity graphs for pathfinding or AI (graph of connected rooms, etc.).

The dungeon gen module should have a function like `generateDungeon(seed, params) -> DungeonMap`. A random seed ensures repeatability if needed. `params` could include desired map size, theme (which could influence tile types and algorithm choice), and difficulty (affecting number of rooms or traps). 

**Example Algorithm:** A simple but effective technique is:
1. Randomly place a number of **rooms** (rectangular areas of floor) in the grid without overlapping.
2. Connect these rooms with **corridors**. For example, take each pair of subsequent rooms and carve a corridor (digging straight lines that meet in a hallway or using a winding tunnel algorithm).
3. Optionally, add **maze-like passages** in empty areas, or sprinkle some loops by connecting random rooms, to ensure multiple paths (avoiding a tree that can be boring).
4. Place special features: doors at room entrances, stairs, treasure rooms, traps, etc., according to probability rules.

This is similar to classic roguelike level generation (e.g., Angband’s algorithm of random non-overlapping rooms then connecting with corridors) improved with some extra loops for non-linearity【13†L139-L147】【13†L169-L177】. We can also incorporate other patterns – e.g., fill everything with a maze then “unmaze” some dead-ends to create pockets for rooms【13†L185-L193】, or use Binary Space Partitioning to systematically subdivide space for rooms.

**Code Prototype:** Below is a simplified Python example of dungeon generation using a rooms-and-corridors approach. This function creates a grid, carves a few rooms, and connects them with corridors. (In a real engine, this would be more sophisticated and use the engine’s random utilities and map classes.)

```python
import random

WALL, FLOOR = '#', '.'

def generate_dungeon(width, height, room_count):
    # Initialize grid with all walls
    grid = [[WALL for _ in range(width)] for _ in range(height)]
    rooms = []
    for _ in range(room_count):
        # Random room size
        rw = random.randint(3, 7)
        rh = random.randint(3, 7)
        # Random position (leave 1-tile border of walls)
        rx = random.randint(1, width - rw - 1)
        ry = random.randint(1, height - rh - 1)
        # Check overlap with existing rooms
        overlap = False
        for (ox, oy, ow, oh) in rooms:
            if not (rx+rw < ox or rx > ox+ow or ry+rh < oy or ry > oy+oh):
                overlap = True
                break
        if overlap:
            continue  # skip this room if it overlaps
        # Carve out the room area
        for x in range(rx, rx+rw):
            for y in range(ry, ry+rh):
                grid[y][x] = FLOOR
        rooms.append((rx, ry, rw, rh))
    # Connect rooms with corridors (naive method: connect centers in order)
    rooms.sort(key=lambda r: (r[0], r[1]))  # sort by position for deterministic chaining
    for i in range(1, len(rooms)):
        x1, y1, w1, h1 = rooms[i-1]
        x2, y2, w2, h2 = rooms[i]
        # Compute center of room i-1 and i
        cx1, cy1 = x1 + w1//2, y1 + h1//2
        cx2, cy2 = x2 + w2//2, y2 + h2//2
        # Dig horizontal tunnel then vertical (or vice versa)
        for x in range(min(cx1, cx2), max(cx1, cx2)+1):
            grid[cy1][x] = FLOOR
        for y in range(min(cy1, cy2), max(cy1, cy2)+1):
            grid[y][cx2] = FLOOR
    return grid

# Example usage:
dungeon_map = generate_dungeon(width=30, height=15, room_count=6)
print("\n".join("".join(row) for row in dungeon_map))
```

*In this snippet:* We randomize rectangular rooms and carve them, ensuring no overlap. Then we connect consecutive rooms with an L-shaped corridor. This produces a basic playable map (represented with `#` for walls and `.` for floor). A real implementation would add more features (doors at the bends, maybe T-junctions, etc.), but this is enough to test the concept. You can run this in a Python environment to see ASCII output of a random dungeon.

The dungeon generation module can be extended with **procedural rules** for specific biomes or themes. For example, a “cyberpunk” theme might generate a city grid instead of random caves (a different algorithm), and a “dark fantasy” theme might add more loops and secret rooms. Rather than separate hard-coded generators, we’d use configurable rules. Bob Nystrom notes that it’s wise to design one generator with many tweakable parameters to produce multiple area styles without rewriting from scratch【13†L119-L127】. We might implement this by having a base algorithm with tunable inputs (e.g., density of rooms, corridor style, sparseness of loops) or by composing smaller algorithmic steps that can be toggled on/off per theme. All these settings would be data-driven (perhaps in a JSON defining “biome” or “dungeon theme” profiles). This satisfies the goal that no specific level layout is hard-coded – it’s all rule-driven and thus unpredictable yet controlled by parameters.

## Loot & Item Generation Module

**Purpose:** The loot system is responsible for creating items – whether found in chests, dropped by enemies, crafted by the player, or rolled from a gacha pull. It must support a **component-based item design with affixes**, to allow millions of possible item combinations. No item is pre-defined; instead, items are assembled from procedural parts (materials, prefixes, suffixes, etc.) following certain rules. This ensures that content remains fresh and supports emergent strategies (players might discover powerful synergies between item traits that designers didn’t explicitly script).

**Item Composition:** We design items as a combination of **components** and **affixes**:
- *Components* are the base parts of an item. For example, a sword could have a `Blade` component and a `Hilt` component. Each component brings certain stats or properties. In a sci-fi setting, a gun might have a `Barrel`, `Stock`, and `Ammunition` as components. Components can be thought of like “item modules” – e.g., a *blade component* might define damage and material (iron, steel, etc.), while a *hilt component* defines weight or durability. The game’s item database will list possible components for each kind of item.
- *Affixes* are modifiers added on top of the base item (prefixes/suffixes in ARPG terms). An affix might add an elemental damage type (“Flaming Sword”), a stat boost (“Ancient Sword” gives +5 attack), or even special abilities (“Vampiric Sword” heals the wielder on hit). Affixes themselves are procedural in that they can have tiers or random values within ranges.

When generating a random item, the loot module will essentially **roll from tables**: first pick a base item type or components, then determine if affixes are added based on rarity, then pick affixes from their respective pools. This is analogous to how games like Diablo do it – in fact, Diablo’s system can be seen as having a loot table for base items and another for affixes, with multiple random rolls to decide what drops and with which modifiers【17†L287-L295】【17†L300-L307】. A drop algorithm might look like:
1. Roll to decide *if* an item drops at all and what *rarity* it is (common, magic, rare, legendary, etc.). This probability can depend on context (e.g., boss chests guarantee at least one rare).
2. Based on rarity, determine how many components or affixes the item will have. (Common might be a single component item with no affix, rare might have two components and one affix, legendary might have unique properties.)
3. Choose base components appropriate for the item category. For example, if the category is “sword”, randomly select one blade component and one hilt component from the component list. These components could themselves have a rarity weighting.
4. Assemble base item stats from the components (e.g., sum or combine the stats provided by each part). This yields the base item (say “Iron Sword” if blade is iron and hilt is generic).
5. If the item is of magic/rare rarity, roll one or more affixes from the affix pool. Affixes may be grouped by type or rarity as well (e.g., powerful affixes only appear on rare+). For each affix, apply its effects to the item’s stats or give it abilities. For instance, a “Flaming” affix might add +3 fire damage and mark the item’s damage type as Fire.
6. Give the item a generated name reflecting its components and affixes (e.g., “Ancient Iron Longsword of Flames”).

All these steps are done through data-driven tables. As an example, a **loot table** for base items might list: Swords (blade+hilt), Axes (head+haft), Bows (limb+string), etc. Each component type list (blade, hilt, etc.) contains entries like *iron blade (+8 damage)*, *steel blade (+12 damage)*, *oak hilt (+2 stability)*, *ebony hilt (+5 stability)*, etc., each possibly with a weight influencing drop chance. A separate **affix table** contains entries like *“Flaming” (adds fire damage, element=Fire)*, *“Vampiric” (adds life steal property)*, *“Swift” (+speed)*, etc., again with their own rarities or prerequisites. This two-table approach is exactly how many ARPGs generate loot【17†L287-L295】【17†L300-L307】 – it allows a huge combination space by mixing base templates with modifiable affixes. Notably, affixes can be very creative (e.g. “spawn flying monkeys on hit” as a hypothetical affix effect【17†L300-L307】), which underscores the need for the engine to handle arbitrary effects in a modular way. In our design, each affix could correspond to a small script or function that is applied to the item or triggers on certain events (this ties in with the Magic system or scripting).

**Crafting and Disassembly:** The crafting system is essentially the inverse of item generation. If a player disassembles an item, we can yield its components (e.g., breaking down an Iron Sword returns an Iron Blade component and an Oak Hilt component). Crafting an item could allow the player to manually combine components – e.g., choose a blade and a hilt from ones they have collected to forge a new sword. This is naturally supported by the component-based item model. Additionally, affixes might be transferrable or re-rollable via crafting (for example, an enchantment table could let players add a random affix to an item). All these actions invoke the loot module’s logic under the hood (e.g., crafting is a deterministic variant of item generation, whereas looting is random generation).

**Interface:** We can implement the loot system as a service with functions like:
- `generate_item(category, rarity) -> Item`: Generate a new Item object of given category (sword, armor, potion, etc.) and rarity. This function would encapsulate the random rolls described above.
- `disassemble_item(item) -> [components]`: Returns the base components from an item.
- `craft_item(components..., affix_choices...) -> Item`: Combines given components into a new item, optionally with specific affixes if allowed.
- `roll_gacha(pool) -> Item`: Perhaps picks an item from a predefined gacha pool (which itself defines drop rates of categories/rarities).

**Code Prototype:** Below is a simplified example showing how an item might be generated from components and affixes in Python. We use placeholder data to illustrate the concept:

blades = [

    {"id": "blade_steel", "name": "Steel Blade", "stats": {"damage": 12}, "material": "Steel"}
]
hilts = [
    {"id": "hilt_oak", "name": "Oak Hilt", "stats": {"stability": 2}, "material": "Oak"},
    {"id": "hilt_ebony", "name": "Ebony Hilt", "stats": {"stability": 5}, "material": "Ebony"}
]
affixes = [
    {"id": "affix_flaming", "name": "Flaming", "effect": {"element": "Fire", "bonus_damage": 3}},
    {"id": "affix_vampiric", "name": "Vampiric", "effect": {"lifesteal": 5}}
]

def generate_sword():
    # Choose components
    blade = random.choice(blades)
    hilt = random.choice(hilts)
    # Base item stats combine blade and hilt stats
    base_damage = blade["stats"].get("damage", 0)
    base_stability = hilt["stats"].get("stability", 0)
    item = {
        "name": f"{blade['material']} Sword",  # start with base name
        "damage": base_damage,
        "stability": base_stability,
        "element": None,
        "effects": []
    }
    # Randomly decide affix (50% chance for demo)
    if random.random() < 0.5:
        affix = random.choice(affixes)
        item["name"] = f"{affix['name']} {item['name']}"  # e.g. "Flaming Iron Sword"
        # Apply affix effects
        if "bonus_damage" in affix["effect"]:
            item["damage"] += affix["effect"]["bonus_damage"]
        if "element" in affix["effect"]:
            item["element"] = affix["effect"]["element"]
        if "lifesteal" in affix["effect"]:
            item["effects"].append(f"lifesteal_{affix['effect']['lifesteal']}%")

# Generate a random sword
for _ in range(3):
    sword = generate_sword()
    print(sword)

In the actual engine, items would be proper objects in the ECS (with components like DamageComponent, maybe an ElementalComponent for the fire property, etc.), rather than dictionaries.

**Affix Logic & Elemental Combat:** Affixes often tie into elemental damage or status effects, which leads into **elemental combat mechanics**. The engine should define a set of elements (e.g. Fire, Water, Lightning, Earth, etc.) and rules for how they interact. For example, fire damage might ignite flammable targets (setting a burn status), water might extinguish fire but also conduct electricity (if something is wet, lightning does more damage), and so on. This rock-paper-scissors of elements should be managed by either the Combat module or a dedicated ElementSystem. We ensure that affixes and spells hook into this system rather than having isolated logic. For instance, a “Flaming” affix could simply tag the item’s attacks with Fire element; the elemental system then knows fire attacks cause burns and deal extra damage to e.g. ice-aligned creatures but less to water-aligned ones. 

The principle is to keep these interactions **systemic**. A famous example is *Breath of the Wild*’s approach: they implemented a “Chemistry Engine” that defines how elements and materials affect each other (fire burns wood, water puts out fire, metal conducts electricity, wind spreads fire, etc.), yielding *multiplicative gameplay* where simple rules produce many emergent effects【23†L79-L88】【23†L92-L100】. We aim for a similar design. Every material (terrain or item) could have properties like *flammable*, *conductive*, *corrosive*, etc., and every element (fire, lightning, acid, etc.) has defined effects on those materials. When an elemental effect occurs (from a spell or affix or potion), the engine checks these rules: e.g., a fire spell hitting a wooden floor tile will set it ablaze (turning it into a fire tile that spreads), whereas a fire spell hitting a stone wall just leaves a scorch mark. This cross-system interaction (Magic affecting Terrain via Physics) is a prime example of emergent complexity – the player might, for instance, intentionally set a room’s floor on fire to damage pursuing enemies or burn down a wooden barricade. None of these are scripted one-off events; they all follow from consistent simulation rules.

## Turn-Based Combat Module

**Purpose:** The combat system governs encounters between the player and enemies in a **turn-based, tile-based** manner. Turn-based combat is ideal for a dungeon crawler as it gives players time for tactical decisions and integrates well with grid movement. Our combat should exemplify the *“four virtues”* of good tactical combat, especially **emergent complexity** (rich tactics from simple rules) and **clarity** (predictable outcomes)【21†L55-L63】. 

**Structure:** We assume a *roguelike-like* model where time is discretized into turns. Typically, the player takes an action (move, attack, cast a spell, use item) which consumes their turn, then enemies take their actions, and so on (either all enemies act or they have their own initiative order). The combat module will manage this turn sequence, as well as turn scheduling (some actions might consume multiple ticks, etc., though a simpler approach is each action is one turn).

**Integration with ECS:** Each entity (player or enemy) in combat will have components like `Position(x,y)`, `Stats{ HP, attack, defense, etc. }`, maybe an `ActionComponent` (to store what action they intend to do or have done), and possibly a reference to AI or player controller. The Combat system will likely loop through entities in initiative order and process their actions. It will query the world (via the dungeon map for movement validity, via the item system for weapon damage, etc.) and update entity components (like reducing HP, etc.).

**Turn Order & Initiative:** For simplicity, we might start with a fixed round-robin: player goes, then each enemy in some order. A more advanced system could assign an initiative value each turn (perhaps based on speed stats or random rolls), or even use a timeline where faster actors act more frequently. Initially, a straightforward queue is fine. This module could provide functions like `next_turn()` to advance to the next entity, `player_action(action)` to submit a player decision, etc. It also should handle end-of-combat conditions (all enemies defeated or player dead).

**Combat Actions and Rules:** The rules should remain as simple as possible but allow combination:
- Movement: moving to an adjacent tile (if free). If moving into a tile occupied by an enemy, that could be treated as an attack or collision.
- Basic Attack: using equipped weapon or natural attack to damage a target in range (melee range for adjacent, or ranged if you have a bow/spell).
- Use Item: e.g., drink potion or throw a bomb.
- Cast Spell: using the magic system (discussed below).

When an attack happens, the Combat system calculates damage. This might involve:
  - Attacker’s attack stat + weapon damage + possible elemental bonus (from affixes or spells).
  - Target’s defense stat or resistances.
  - Random factor if any (we might include a small damage range or critical hits, unless we want fully deterministic combat for clarity).
  - If the attack has an elemental type, apply the elemental interaction rules (for example, if target has a status making them weak to that element, amplify damage; or if target is immune, reduce damage).
  - Create a damage event: reduce target HP and trigger any on-hit effects (like life steal affix would heal the attacker, a poison weapon might add a poison status component to target, etc.).

Because we want **clarity**, the system should probably surface the expected damage or hit chance to the player in the UI before they commit (as many tactics games do). We can ensure rules are not overly convoluted – e.g., avoid too many hidden modifiers.

**Enemy AI in Combat:** On their turn, enemies need to decide on an action. This falls to the AI module, but the Combat system can interface with it. For example, Combat can call something like `action = AI.decide_action(enemy, game_state)` for each enemy, then execute that action. A simple AI might move toward the player if not in range, or attack if in range. More advanced behavior could be scripted per enemy type (some might flee when hurt, others use special abilities). We keep the AI logic separate, but it operates within the combat turn structure.

**Example Turn Loop Code:** Here is a pseudo-code outline of how the turn-based loop might be managed:

```python
turn_entities = [player] + enemies  # list of entities in combat
turn_index = 0

while combat_is_active:
    entity = turn_entities[turn_index]
    if entity == player:
        action = player.get_player_input()  # e.g., move or attack chosen by player
    else:
        action = AI.decide_action(entity, game_state)
    combat.execute_action(entity, action)
    # Check end conditions (e.g., someone died, remove them from turn order if so)
    if player.hp <= 0:
        combat.game_over(player_dead=True)
        break
    if all(enemy.hp <= 0 for enemy in enemies):
        combat.end_encounter(victory=True)
        break
    # Advance to next turn
    turn_index = (turn_index + 1) % len(turn_entities)
```

In a real implementation, `execute_action` would contain the logic to handle each action type (movement, attack, spell, etc.) and integrate with the physics (for movement collision), map (for line-of-sight or range), and items (for damage stats). Also, initiative could be recalculated each round rather than a static list.

**Emergent Combat Features:** With all systems in play, we want combat to allow creative tactics. Thanks to our modular systems, combat isn’t just trading sword blows:
- Players can leverage **physics**: e.g., push an enemy off a ledge (if terrain physics supports height), or topple a column to crush monsters. If the physics system detects a falling object hit, it could create a damage event that Combat processes.
- **Magic and elements** play a huge role in emergent tactics: create a water pool via a spell then zap it with lightning to hit all enemies standing in it; or use wind to spread a poison gas cloud toward enemies, etc. The combination of spells with environmental effects (and AI that isn't explicitly told how to react in every scenario) yields unplanned outcomes, which is the essence of emergent gameplay.
- **AI behavior** combined with other systems: e.g., monsters might have simple rules like “avoid fire if on fire” so they run in panic – which the player could exploit to herd them. Or a monster might accidentally step on a trap while pathing to the player.

To achieve this, the Combat system doesn’t need special cases for each scenario – it just needs to process the results of other systems. For example, if an enemy is standing on a tile that the FireSystem has marked as burning, the Combat system could simply apply fire damage to anything on that tile each turn. This again shows the importance of the ECS/event design: the FireSystem might raise an event “tile_burning” that Combat listens for to decrement HP of entities on that tile, or the entity might have a Burning status component that Combat/StatusSystem reduces HP from each turn. By sharing a consistent world state (tile states, status components), each system’s straightforward rules intersect to create rich outcomes.

## Magic System (Haloic Language)

**Purpose:** The magic system allows for casting spells, which are defined via the **Haloic language**, a custom scripting/DSL for magic in this engine. Rather than hard-coding spells (“Fireball does X damage in radius Y”), we implement a flexible spell definition language that designers or modders (and possibly players, if you expose it) can use to create new spells and effects. This not only supports modding but also deep player experimentation – if appropriate, players could literally script or assemble spells in-game by combining runes or incantations.

**Haloic Language Design:** The Haloic language could be a high-level, human-readable scripting format for spells. For example, it might allow describing a spell’s behavior in terms of primitive actions:
- creating projectiles,
- applying elemental effects to areas,
- altering entity stats,
- conditional effects, etc.

We might design it as a simple JSON or text DSL that the engine parses. For instance, a fireball spell might be defined in Haloic as something like:
```
spell "Fireball":
    cost 5 mana
    effect:
       create_projectile { speed:10, sprite:"fireball.png" }
       on_hit:
          area_explosion { radius:2, damage:20, element:Fire }
```
This is a hypothetical syntax, but it illustrates that the spell is composed of smaller effect building blocks (projectile, explosion, damage, elemental tag). The Magic system would interpret this at runtime: when the player casts "Fireball", the system reads the definition, spawns a projectile entity moving forward; when it hits something or reaches the target tile, it triggers an explosion area effect dealing fire damage.

We can implement the Haloic language in a few ways:
- **Interpretation:** Write a parser that reads the spell scripts and constructs a sequence of engine commands (like spawn entity, deal damage, etc.). This could be as simple as reading a JSON and calling appropriate module functions.
- **Compilation to data**: Convert the script into a structured data (like an object with fields like `on_hit_effects`) for faster execution.
- **Use existing scripting**: We could embed a known scripting language (Lua, Python, Angelscript, etc.) and just provide an API for spells. But since the prompt specifically says “via Haloic language”, we assume a custom or domain-specific approach, which might be more limited but tailored for magic.

**Integration:** The Magic system will likely interface with Combat and Physics. A spell cast is an action in combat, but its effects can be physical (moving objects, creating fire on tiles) or directly damage (which goes through combat’s damage logic). So Magic might produce entities or status effects that then get handled by other systems:
- E.g., summoning spell: Magic spawns a new creature entity with certain components (and the Combat system will then include it in turn order perhaps).
- Terrain-altering spell: Magic could modify the DungeonMap (turn tile at (x,y) into water or lava).
- Buff/Debuff spell: Magic could add a status component to an entity (like “Strengthened” or “Frozen”), which the Combat/Status system then applies over time.

**Haloic as Modding Interface:** Because spells are written in an external language, adding a new spell is as easy as dropping a new script in the data folder. The engine would load all spells definitions on startup (or on the fly) and register them (perhaps giving each an ID or name). The game could even allow players to combine elemental runes at runtime to form Haloic spell sequences (imagine a system where the player combines the runes for "fire" + "explosion" to create a fireball spell – essentially constructing a Haloic script on the fly).

**Example Implementation Note:** For initial testing, we might not implement a full parser but can simulate one. For instance, we can create a function `cast_spell(spell_name, caster, target)` that looks up a predefined dictionary of effects. For a Fireball, it might directly call a projectile creation function and then schedule an explosion. The Haloic DSL would come in a later iteration once the underlying effect functions (projectile movement, area damage, etc.) are in place.

*Code sketch:* Suppose we represent a very simple “language” where each spell is just a structured dict (in practice this could come from a JSON or builder API):

```python
# Example of simplistic internal representation of a spell
spells = {
    "Fireball": {
        "cost": 5,
        "on_cast": lambda caster, target: create_projectile(caster, target, speed=10, sprite="fire.png"),
        "on_hit": lambda projectile, hit_target: area_explosion(center=hit_target.pos, radius=2, damage=20, element="Fire")
    }
}

def cast_spell(name, caster, target):
    spell = spells[name]
    if caster.mana < spell["cost"]:
        print("Not enough mana!")
        return
    caster.mana -= spell["cost"]
    print(f"{caster.name} casts {name}!")
    projectile = spell["on_cast"](caster, target)
    projectile.on_hit = spell["on_hit"]
```

In this pseudo-code, we stored the logic in lambdas for brevity. In reality, the Haloic script would describe what to do and the Magic system would perform those actions. The `projectile.on_hit` could be set so that when the Physics system detects a collision, it calls that function, causing an explosion effect. This demonstrates the interplay: Magic system initiates something, Physics detects the outcome (impact), then Magic (or Combat) applies damage.

Overall, the Magic/Haloic module initially will involve designing the scripting format and hooking into existing systems. For immediate testing, one could hardcode a couple of example spells like above and cast them in-game to see if the effects trigger correctly. The full parsing of a custom language might be a later development step, but planning for it now (what kinds of primitives we need: create entities, apply status, etc.) guides how we build the underlying engine functions.

## Enemy AI Module

**Purpose:** The AI module controls non-player entities (monsters, NPCs) in both exploration and combat. It should be modular and data-driven so that adding a new enemy type with distinct behavior does not require engine changes, only configuration or scripting of that behavior. 

**Behavior Architectures:** We can use **finite state machines (FSM)** or **behavior trees** for enemies. For example, a simple FSM for a monster might have states: Patrol (wander), Chase (if player seen), Attack (if in range), Flee (if low health), etc. Transitions between states are triggered by conditions (see player, lose player, etc.). This could be encoded in a small AI script or data file per enemy type:
```json
"goblin_ai": {
  "states": ["Idle", "Chase", "Attack", "Flee"],
  "transitions": [
    {"from":"Idle", "to":"Chase", "condition": "see_player"},
    {"from":"Chase", "to":"Attack", "condition": "distance_to_player < 1"},
    {"from":"Attack", "to":"Chase", "condition": "distance_to_player > 1"},
    {"from":"Any", "to":"Flee", "condition": "hp < 20%"}
  ]
}
```
This is one way to represent it. Alternatively, a behavior tree could be scripted in code or a small DSL.

**Pathfinding:** The AI will typically need to pathfind through the dungeon. We can utilize A* or a simpler flood-fill on the grid to have enemies move towards the player (or to waypoints). This is part of the AI module or a shared Pathfinding utility. Because our dungeon maps can be non-trivial (rooms, corridors, obstacles), implementing A* on the tile grid (with walls as unwalkable, maybe doors as something they can open) is essential. This too should be modular – for instance, if one wanted to swap in a more advanced pathfinding (like funnel algorithm or consider dynamic obstacles), they could replace the pathfinding component.

**Senses:** To create believable behavior, AI should have notions of **vision (line-of-sight)** and possibly **hearing**. The fog-of-war system can be leveraged for AI: just as we track what the player has seen, we can track what each enemy can “see” (though usually simpler: if player is not in direct LOS and within some radius, enemy doesn’t notice them). We can implement a line-of-sight check on the grid (e.g. raycast or Bresenham line) to determine if walls block view. Stealth or noise could be future enhancements (sound propagation on grid).

**Execution within Engine:** The Combat system calls AI decisions during turn-based fights as described. But even outside of combat (when the player is exploring), monsters might still wander or take actions. If the game runs in turns even during exploration (as many roguelikes do), it’s effectively the same loop (player turn, then all monsters turns). If not, and exploration is real-time until combat starts (like some games where monsters move in real-time until you enter tactical mode), the engine would need to handle both modes. A simpler approach is everything is turn-based by nature (every step the player takes is a turn for monsters too), which many classic roguelikes use.

**Example:** To test AI, one can drop a couple of monsters in the generated dungeon and simulate a few turns:
- Place a goblin at some coordinates.
- Each turn, have it decide movement: if it has line of sight to player, move closer (pathfind one step toward). If not, maybe wander randomly.
- See if it eventually reaches and “attacks” the player (which could just be printing a message for now).

Pseudo-code for a very basic AI decision (for a chasing enemy):
```python
def decide_action(monster, game_state):
    player = game_state.player
    if can_see(monster, player):
        if distance(monster.pos, player.pos) <= 1:
            return ("attack", player)
        else:
            next_step = pathfind_step(monster.pos, player.pos, game_state.map)
            return ("move", next_step)
    else:
        # Can't see player: wander or stand idle
        if random.random() < 0.5:
            return ("move", monster.pos.random_adjacent())
        else:
            return ("wait", None)
```
This is oversimplified (monsters have perfect knowledge once they see player, etc.), but it suffices to test the pipeline. In practice, we can refine and also incorporate different tactics (e.g., ranged enemies will not move closer if in range, etc., which could be encoded in their data).

Because the AI module is separate, one could mod in a completely different behavior by providing a new `decide_action` script for a monster. For example, a mod could implement a “coward” AI that always flees from player, or a “turret” AI that never moves but shoots when player is in sight. The engine just calls whatever logic is attached to that entity’s AI component.

## Terrain Physics & Interaction Module

**Purpose:** This module handles the physical simulation aspects of the world – primarily collisions (walls blocking movement), forces (if any), and interactions of objects with the environment. In a top-down 2D dungeon crawler, “physics” isn’t as prominent as in a platformer, but we still have important physics-like features:
- **Collision detection:** The player and creatures should not walk through walls or solid objects. The physics module will check intended moves (from the Combat or input system) and prevent or slide accordingly. This is essentially tile collision (the dungeon map can quickly tell if a tile is passable or not).
- **Rigid body physics for objects:** If the game includes pushable barrels, falling rocks, or projectile trajectories, a physics engine can simulate those. For example, a thrown object or projectile might arc through the air (with gravity) – in 2D top-down, we might not simulate gravity unless we have the notion of height. But if we include height (even just conceptually for jumps or flying), a physics sim could be involved.
- **Terrain effect physics:** Liquids flowing, fire spreading, etc., can be considered part of physics/chemistry simulation. The earlier discussion on elemental interactions (the “Chemistry Engine” idea【23†L79-L88】) lies at the intersection of physics and magic. For instance, spreading fire to nearby flammable tiles each turn can be seen as a physics/chemistry rule.
- **Materials and Damage:** The physics module might also handle destruction of terrain or objects. For example, an explosion (from Magic or a bomb item) might tell Physics “apply explosion at (x,y) with force F”. Physics can calculate which walls or entities are within range, apply knockback to entities (moving them on the grid or applying a stun status) and possibly break walls if they are destructible. Each terrain tile could have a durability or material type which determines if it can break (wooden barricade vs stone wall).
- **Gravity and Falling:** If we choose to incorporate verticality (even lightly), the physics could manage gravity – e.g., a trap door opens and something falls to a lower level, or a levitation spell counteracts gravity. But for now, we can keep things mostly 2D.

**Implementation:** Depending on the framework, we might integrate a physics library (Phaser has Arcade/Matter.js, MonoGame could use Farseer physics, etc.). However, a full continuous physics engine might be overkill for grid-based movement. We can implement simpler grid physics:
- Represent impassable tiles and use collision checks when moving.
- For projectiles, simulate their path tile by tile (or use continuous if using a physics lib for nice trajectories).
- For forces like knockback, perhaps treat them as special movements (if an explosion hits an entity, attempt to move it X tiles away from center, stopping if a wall is encountered).
- For fire, water, etc., implement cellular automata or wave propagation on the grid (spread to neighboring tiles over time).

**Emergent Interactions through Physics:** This module is critical for emergent behavior. By giving physical properties to objects and environments, players can invent solutions. For example:
- **Destroying Terrain:** If a spell or bomb can blow up walls, players might shortcut a dungeon or trap monsters behind rubble.
- **Environmental Hazards:** Water on floor making it slippery (maybe causing movement to overshoot), or oil spills that can ignite, etc.
- **Object Interactions:** Perhaps players can push crates to block a passage (AI then has to break it or go around) or stack items to climb (if we allowed climbing mechanic).
- **Elemental Reactions:** As discussed, this is part of physics/chemistry – e.g., an *electric shock* in water could propagate in that water area and stun all creatures touching it; strong *wind* could push gas clouds or extinguish flames.

All these require the physics system to track the state (tiles with water, tiles on fire, etc.) and apply rules. We can store a state for each tile (like a component of the tile entity) indicating if it contains a fluid or fire or other transient effect, plus maybe a timer. 

**Testing Physics:** We can start small by testing simple collisions and tile changes. For instance:
- Ensure the player cannot walk through walls (the movement code in Combat calls Physics to check the target tile).
- Test a simple “explosion” function that turns nearby floor tiles into fire tiles and see if that state is tracked.
- Simulate one step of fire spreading: if a tile is on fire and an adjacent tile is flammable, after a turn that adjacent tile catches fire.

These are straightforward to simulate via grid updates.

*Example:* A rudimentary fire spread in Python (assuming we mark flammable tiles):
```python
flammable = set()  # set of (x,y) coords that are flammable (e.g., wood floor tiles)
fire_tiles = set()  # currently burning tiles

def spread_fire():
    new_fires = set()
    for (x,y) in list(fire_tiles):
        for (nx, ny) in neighbors(x,y):
            if (nx,ny) in flammable and (nx,ny) not in fire_tiles:
                new_fires.add((nx,ny))
    # all new flammable neighbors catch fire
    fire_tiles.update(new_fires)

# Example usage: set a starting fire and spread for a few steps
fire_tiles.add((10, 5))
for t in range(3):
    spread_fire()
    print(f"After {t+1} spread steps: {fire_tiles}")
```
This would show the fire region growing outwards. In the engine, when an entity is on a tile that becomes fire, that entity would receive a Burning status (handled by Combat/Status systems). Likewise, if a water spell douses a tile, the Physics system might remove it from `fire_tiles` set (and maybe create a steam cloud as a new effect – demonstrating element interactions).

We also plan to integrate **post-processing** or visual effects for these physics interactions (e.g., shader for heat distortion on burning tiles, etc.), but that’s handled in rendering.

## Rendering & Fog-of-War Module

**Purpose:** The rendering module draws the game world and applies visual effects. It needs to handle:
- **Tilemap rendering:** Drawing the dungeon floor/walls efficiently (possibly using a tilemap to batch draw).
- **Sprite rendering:** Drawing characters, monsters, items (could be pixel art or minimal animations).
- **Lighting and Post-processing:** If we include lighting, shadows, or post-process (bloom, color filters for themes, screen shake on explosions, etc.).
- **Fog of War:** Darkening unexplored or out-of-vision areas of the map.

**Graphics Approach:** Given we aim for pixel/voxel styles, we likely use pixel art textures for tiles and sprites. The engine might allow swapping tilesets for different themes (cyberpunk tiles vs fantasy tiles). For “voxel” support, one approach is to use a 2.5D perspective or dynamically constructed tile meshes if using a 3D engine – but since we are focusing 2D, it might just mean blocky aesthetics or possibly using an engine that can do both 2D and 3D (MonoGame can, Phaser is 2D only unless using 3D plugins).

**Biome Blending & Seamless Tiling:** To avoid harsh edges between different terrain types (say grass to desert biome in an overworld, or lava area to normal area in a dungeon), the rendering system can use *autotiling* techniques. This means choosing the correct tile variant depending on neighbors (for example, a tile that is half grass half sand at the border). We can prepare tilesets that include transitional tiles and let the engine pick them based on adjacency rules. Some engines have built-in support for this (e.g., 47-tile blob autotile in RPG Maker or Godot). Alternatively, we can implement a simple rule: for each tile, look at its neighbors and pick a sprite index that visually blends. We might not need full alpha blending if we have pre-made blend tiles.

For **voxel look**, if required, we might simulate it by drawing tiles with shadows or slight 3D extrusion, or actually use a 3D cube representation for tiles (which is more complex). Possibly out of scope for initial implementation, but the architecture should allow plugging in a different renderer that, for example, draws each tile as a voxel cube if desired.

**Fog of War Implementation:** Fog-of-war means the player can only see areas within their line-of-sight (and possibly a memory of seen areas). We maintain a 2D boolean array `visible[y][x]` for whether each tile is currently visible. This is updated whenever the player (or other vision sources like allies) moves:
- We perform a **field-of-view (FOV)** calculation from the player’s position, marking all tiles visible that are within a certain radius and not blocked by walls. There are known algorithms for this (shadow-casting, ray casting in octants, etc.). To start, we could even use a simple radius diamond or circle for visibility, then refine to actual line-of-sight.
- Tiles that are visible get marked as seen. We might also keep a `explored[y][x]` to remember if a tile was ever seen (so we can reveal it on map but draw it dark when not currently visible).
- The renderer then draws visible tiles normally, draws previously seen but not currently visible tiles in a dimmed overlay (foggy), and completely unseen tiles as black (or not at all).

This system ties in with AI (monsters could be invisible if not in FOV, unless we simulate sound).

For initial testing, we can simulate a very simple FOW: e.g., reveal a square or circle around the player. Below is an example using our earlier dungeon generation to illustrate fog of war. We place a player and reveal tiles around them:

```python
# Assume dungeon_map from earlier generation and player position (px, py)
width, height = len(dungeon_map[0]), len(dungeon_map)
visible = [[False]*width for _ in range(height)]

def reveal_area(cx, cy, r=3):
    for y in range(max(0, cy-r), min(height, cy+r+1)):
        for x in range(max(0, cx-r), min(width, cx+r+1)):
            # simple circular radius check
            if (x-cx)**2 + (y-cy)**2 <= r*r:
                visible[y][x] = True

# Initial reveal around player
reveal_area(player.x, player.y, r=3)

# Print map with fog (unseen as blank)
for y in range(height):
    row = ""
    for x in range(width):
        if not visible[y][x]:
            row += " "
        else:
            # show P for player, or tile char
            if x == player.x and y == player.y:
                row += "P"
            else:
                row += dungeon_map[y][x]
    print(row)
```

This would output the dungeon map with only a small radius around the player visible (P denotes the player). As the player moves, we would call `reveal_area` at the new position, adding more tiles to visible. For actual line-of-sight, one would integrate a ray-cast that stops at walls.

**Rendering Pipeline:** In a real engine (say MonoGame or Phaser), the rendering module might:
- Draw floor tiles layer.
- Draw items/objects (e.g., a chest or potion on ground).
- Draw characters/monsters.
- Apply lighting/fog: one way is to have a black semi-transparent overlay covering the whole map, and carve holes (or set alpha=0) in that overlay for visible tiles. Many roguelikes do this by rendering a black mask and updating a texture each time FOV changes. Alternatively, shader-based approaches can use a texture of visibility.
- UI/HUD on top (health bars, inventory).

We also ensure our rendering can support **post-processing** like screen shake, flashes (for lightning spells), color tint (maybe entering a cyberpunk area adds a neon glow shader). These are icing on the cake, but our architecture allows the rendering module to take cues from events (e.g., on "explosion" event, trigger screen shake effect).

**Theme Variation:** Supporting different aesthetics might mean swapping sprite sheets and possibly shader parameters. For instance, a cyberpunk tileset might come with its own autotiling rules (neon connectors instead of cave walls). We can abstract the rendering so that the dungeon generator tags tiles with logical types (floor, wall, door, water) and the rendering module looks up the correct sprite for the current theme. E.g., a tile of type “wall” in theme “SciFi” might correspond to a sci-fi wall texture, in “Fantasy” to a stone wall texture. By keeping those mappings in data (maybe a config file per theme), adding a new theme is just adding new art assets and config, not changing code.

## Project Structure & Initial Subsystems Implementation

We now have an overall picture of the engine. To summarize the architecture in terms of code organization:
- **Engine Core**: Initializes modules and manages global loop or event dispatch. Might include the ECS world (entity manager, component storage) if we use ECS.
- **Modules**: Each in its own file or namespace, e.g. `dungeon_gen.py`, `loot_system.py`, `combat.py`, `magic.py`, etc., containing the classes and functions for that subsystem.
- **Data**: JSON or script files defining content (item components, affix lists, enemy stats, spell scripts, theme tile mappings, etc.).
- **Assets**: Sprites, sound, etc., likely organized by theme or type.

A possible directory layout:
```
/engine
    dungeon.py        # dungeon generation
    loot.py           # loot & item generation
    combat.py         # turn-based combat logic
    magic.py          # spell system
    ai.py             # enemy AI behaviors
    physics.py        # collision and environment interactions
    render.py         # rendering and FOV
    ecs.py            # (optional) ECS core if needed
/game
    main.py           # game initialization, main loop
    scenes.py         # maybe for handling game states (menus, game over, etc.)
/data
    items.json        # definitions of item components and affixes
    enemies.json      # enemy types and stats
    spells.halo       # definitions in Haloic language
    themes/           # maybe subfolder for each theme’s config
/assets
    tiles/            # tile images
    sprites/          # character/enemy sprites
    ...
```

This ensures a **single buildable code repo**. We can choose a framework and language; for demonstration we've used Python pseudocode for clarity and quick testing, but the architecture is framework-agnostic. If we were to implement in, say, **MonoGame (C#)**, each module might be a class with Update/Draw methods or a service. In **Phaser 3 (JS)**, we might use separate JS classes for systems and use Phaser’s scene or custom update loop to call them. The key is we maintain clear module boundaries.

**Initial Priorities:** We will start by implementing a vertical slice of the game focusing on:
- Dungeon generation (basic rooms & corridors) – **Test:** generate a level and print or render it.
- Loot system with item generation – **Test:** generate some random items and log them.
- Affix logic – **Test:** ensure affixes modify item stats and possibly that those stats would reflect in combat if used.
- Turn-based combat framework – **Test:** simulate a simple fight between a player and one monster on the generated map (this could be done via console output initially, e.g., player and monster take turns until one is defeated).
- Rendering with fog-of-war – **Test:** display the dungeon map with FOV applied, updating as the player “moves” (even if we just step through a couple of moves in text or simple graphical form).

By getting these subsystems running in a basic form, we can already play a rudimentary dungeon crawl: e.g., spawn player and a monster in the dungeon, allow the player to move with WASD (each move reveals new tiles via FOW and triggers monster turn to move), pick up a generated item, and attack the monster. The output might be text-based for now (or very simple graphics) but it proves the engine loop and module interactions.

Each of these modules can be expanded independently. For instance, once basic combat works, we can add more skills or enemy types easily by adding data and minor logic. Because our foundation is modular, adding a crafting system later might just reuse the loot module’s combination logic. The gacha system might simply call `loot.generate_item` with certain rarities.

**Final Note:** This engine’s design maximizes **iteration speed and modifiability**. Using a high-level framework like Python/Pygame or Love2D for prototyping lets us hot-reload assets and scripts for quick testing. We could even expose a console in-game to tweak parameters (e.g., regenerate dungeon with a different seed). Once the gameplay solidifies, we can port or optimize parts in a more performant environment if needed for mobile. Throughout, the adherence to modular architecture ensures that no system is too tightly coupled – which is crucial for maintaining a complex simulation where unexpected interactions (the fun part of emergent gameplay) can happen without breaking the game. Each piece (dungeon gen, loot, combat, etc.) operates by its own rules, and the magic happens when those rules intersect in novel ways, yielding a rich 2D dungeon crawler experience.
